title: Fear of ICE hinders the rebuilding of California's fire-ravaged zones | U.S. - EL PAÍS English
description:
Before he arrives, he checks social media to make sure there are no Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in the vicinity.
According to Hernández, ICE raids keep crews on alert and scare away those with irregular immigration status.
This fear is not unfounded: ICE has shown up at various construction sites in Altadena and arrested several workers.
“Some believe that white construction workers are going to come and rebuild their house.
However, these three men have refused to go quietly and have filed a lawsuit against the federal government flagging up alleged racist language used by the ICE agents during their arrest.
text:
The sound of hammers, drills and Mexican music herald the rising from the ashes of Altadena. Just over a year ago, only the charred remains of homes blasted by the Eaton wildfires were in evidence. Now, the wooden skeletons of houses are multiplying and gradually recovering their shape. As one of the most devastating wildfires in California’s recent history, it claimed 19 lives, leveled thousands of homes and reduced an entire neighborhood to rubble. But on one construction site, manager Ian Hernández has a task that goes beyond supervising the workers. Before he arrives, he checks social media to make sure there are no Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in the vicinity. That morning, he says, he checked that the coast was clear.

According to Hernández, ICE raids keep crews on alert and scare away those with irregular immigration status. This fear is not unfounded: ICE has shown up at various construction sites in Altadena and arrested several workers. Others have been detained on their way to work. According to organizations that defend migrants, ICE has been seeking undocumented migrants since reconstruction began.

“In February, a car on Mendocina Street let us know that ICE was just around the corner. Some workers hid and others stayed. Nothing happened. It was Friday. On Saturday, no one came to work,” says Hernández, an Oaxacan foreman who supervises the construction of 10 houses. Mendocina Street was one of the last to be engulfed by the Eaton fire in January 2025. It is now part of an area of vacant lots where a middle-class neighborhood once sprawled across the foothills of the Angeles National Forest. Previous fires had never reached so far south.

Almost all the houses being rebuilt in Altadena have chained and padlocked the two-meter-high fences that surround them, even during the working day. “It’s so that ICE doesn’t have access,” explains another foreman. “God willing, they will never come here, and nothing will happen.”

Billboards warn: Do not enter without authorization. Private property. Other factors accounting for the slow progress of reconstruction include bottlenecks in processing permits from the local government, a process that can take up to 125 business days; indemnities from insurers that fail to cover the total cost of construction; and the increase in the cost of materials and labor.

“ICE agents were in Altadena and Pasadena [a neighboring city] for five consecutive days,” says José Madera, director of the Pasadena Community Labor Center, an organization that functions as a safe meeting point for employers and day laborers, as well as cleaners. “The owners of the houses have told us that the builders no longer want to come to work. That affects families because they cannot return to their homes.”

But the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) maintains that ICE raids on workplaces are “a fundamental pillar” of its strategy to protect the public and the country’s economy. The agency also claims it seeks to rescue possible victims of labor trafficking and exploitation. “These operations aim to dismantle illegal employment networks that harm U.S. workers, destabilize labor markets, and threaten communities,” DHS said in a written statement to EL PAÍS.

“I pray they leave them alone”

The new home of African American Damon Blount is half-built. The work began in April and now a crew of construction workers is putting on the roof. It will take eight to 10 months to complete, but Blount is confident his family can settle there before Christmas — that is, if ICE doesn’t show up.

“There are a lot of Hispanic workers in the community right now, and I just pray they leave people alone, that they allow them to rebuild, and that they let us go home,” Blount says. Some of his neighbors have been unlucky. “They said that ICE agents have taken three or four workers, and that has caused delays.”

Immigrant advocacy organizations, media, and politicians have reported ICE raids at construction sites, bus stops, area coffee shops, and at traffic lights. Last January, the day that Altadena commemorated the first anniversary of the Eaton Fire, ICE returned to the streets of the city. “These chaotic raids are never justified, but they are especially cruel when they target our friends and loved ones, including the people who do the physical and specialized work needed to help us recover from this disaster,” said state Senator Sasha Renée Pérez, a Democrat who represents the area.

Volunteers patrol the streets in a bid to detect ICE vehicles, but their efforts have not been enough. “The migra [ICE] comes here often. The agents ride in private cars and it is difficult to identify them,” explains Andrés Rivas, a 70-year-old Salvadoran who is looking to be hired by one of the properties in Altadena. Rivas is a U.S. citizen, but he still fears he could be detained and spend some time in immigration custody. “They come very early. The risk exists,” he says.

A slow business

The resurgence of Altadena, where the Eaton fire destroyed 6,746 homes, has been, above all, lacking in funds. As of June 19, the Los Angeles County government had issued 2,845 building permits, but only 89 homes were habitable. More than 1,600 houses were still under construction, from laying the foundations to the final finishes.

Marialyce Pedersen hopes her home will be ready soon. Right now, there’s just a plot of land. For two decades, she lived in a house in Altadena that she bought from a friend and that, over the years, she filled with memories. Among the most precious were her grandmother’s piano and dozens of children’s books that she dreamed of reading to her grandchildren. Everything went. “It was horrible, it’s the worst thing that has happened to me,” said Pedersen, 62, who has worked as an environmental consultant and adviser to the Walt Disney Company.

Pedersen has already reached out to her trusted builder, a Salvadoran migrant who has been in the U.S. for 25 years. But she fears that he or one of his workers could be detained by ICE, either on her property or at one of the Home Depot stores where they buy materials.

“Some believe that white construction workers are going to come and rebuild their house. Well, good luck with that. It is not going to happen. Hispanic migrants are the ones who are working reconstruction and the ones who are here in our community,” Pedersen says. “They are willing to work, even in this heat.”

The day laborers who never made it to Altadena

Out of nowhere, four pickup trucks screeched to a stop in front of a bus stop next to a coffee shop in Pasadena. Several masked officers got out. It was the morning of June 18, 2025, amid the intensification of raids in the LA metropolitan area — part of the Trump administration’s mass deportation offensive. Among those arrested were three day laborers who were on their way to work on a house in Altadena: Pedro Vázquez Perdomo, Isaac Antonio Villegas Molina, and Carlos Alexander Osorto. The three were handcuffed. One of them, who tried to escape on foot, had a taser pressed to his head. “Stop or I’m going to use it,” the officer shouted, according to court documents.

Instead of arriving in Altadena, the three day laborers ended up in the parking lot of a CVS pharmacy. There, they had their immigration status verified. They were then transferred to the ICE detention center in Adelanto, about 60 miles from L.A. However, these three men have refused to go quietly and have filed a lawsuit against the federal government flagging up alleged racist language used by the ICE agents during their arrest.

Pablo Alvarado, leader of the National Day Laborer Network (NDLON), says that this is one of the clearest examples of how ICE operations are affecting a city that is trying to get back on its feet. “Contractors can’t find enough labor. Although it was said they would not carry out raids here, the migra has been in the vicinity and has detained workers,” Alvarado says. “It’s clear that, in the literal sense, migrants are rebuilding communities and ICE is disrupting this through immoral, inhumane, cruel and illegal operations.”

text:
Tarrant County booking records show that the county booked 278 defendants from January 1 through August 3, 2026, who had U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement holds. The file associates those defendants with 480 coded criminal charge entries apart from the holds, according to county data The Dallas Express obtained.

The spreadsheet contains 497 non-ICE charge rows for those defendants. Of those, 477 name an offense, while three additional rows carry a first-degree felony code without naming the offense. The remaining 17 contain only an “other offense” or administrative description.

Because the export omits case numbers and repeats rows with the same visible fields, the 480 figure counts charge entries as the county supplied them, not 480 confirmed unique cases.

The county marked 355 of the 480 coded entries as first-, second- or third-degree felonies or state jail felonies. The file lists 42 entries for aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, 28 for assault causing bodily injury involving family violence and 26 for assault of a family or household member by impeding breath or circulation.

The records also list 16 entries for sexual assault of a child, five for aggravated sexual assault of a child, 11 for indecency with a child by sexual contact and 10 describing continuous sexual abuse of a child under 14. Other entries include aggravated kidnapping, aggravated robbery and 57 involving driving while intoxicated.

The charges listed in the file represent allegations, not convictions. The law presumes each defendant innocent unless a court enters a conviction. An ICE hold does not establish a conviction or a final removal order. The spreadsheet does not include immigration-court records sufficient to independently determine each person’s final immigration status.

How Tarrant County’s 287(g) program works

The Tarrant County Sheriff’s Office describes its 287(g) partnership with ICE as a jail-based program. The agency says it limits the program to illegal aliens facing high misdemeanor or felony charges.

ICE defines a detainer as a request that a law enforcement agency notify ICE before release and maintain custody temporarily so federal officers can assume custody. The Dallas Express previously reported that Tarrant County has participated in the 287(g) program since 2017.

State Rep. David Lowe (R-District 91) told The Dallas Express that the records demonstrate what he believes is at stake in the political debate over immigration enforcement.

“The Tarrant County data shows exactly what is at stake. ICE holds include illegal aliens charged with sexual assault of a child, kidnapping, and other violent offenses. Democrats are running on abolishing ICE, and that agenda would make Tarrant County families, especially our children, more vulnerable. I stand with ICE and the safety of American families,” Lowe said.

Democratic commissioners opposed ICE grant

Tarrant County commissioners voted 3-2 on February 10 to approve an application for a $140,000 state grant supporting the county’s 287(g) program. Tarrant County Commissioners Alisa Simmons (D-Precinct 2) and Roderick Miles Jr. (D-Precinct 1) opposed the application.

The state grant program covers 287(g) costs that the federal government does not reimburse, including personnel, required reporting, equipment, training and confinement expenses, the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts said.

“I do not support ICE. I do not support this grant, and I do not support expanding immigration enforcement at the county level,” Simmons said during the February 10 meeting.

Simmons also pointed to two recent jail escapes and what she described as 76 deaths in custody. “Tarrant County has its own problems to fix and deal with operationally,” Simmons said.

The Dallas Express contacted Simmons and Miles to ask whether the criminal charges in the records affect their positions on ICE enforcement but did not receive a response by publication.

Section 287(g) agreements allow state and local law enforcement officers to perform certain federal civil immigration enforcement functions.
Why is New York suing the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office?
The Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office has maintained a 287(g) agreement with ICE since March 2020, according to the governor's and attorney general's offices.
After the new law was enacted, the attorney general's office contacted the sheriff's office seeking information about the status of the agreement.
"The Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office has been given every opportunity to follow the law, yet has chosen not to."
text:
Gov. Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James have filed a lawsuit against the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office, alleging it failed to comply with a new state law requiring local law enforcement agencies to end certain agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The lawsuit centers on New York's Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, which required local law enforcement agencies to terminate agreements made under Section 287(g) of the federal Immigration and Nationality Act by Aug. 25, 2026.

The law prohibits local governments and law enforcement agencies from entering into or remaining in such agreements with ICE.

What are 287(g) agreements?

Section 287(g) agreements allow state and local law enforcement officers to perform certain federal civil immigration enforcement functions.

Depending on the terms of an agreement, local officers may be authorized to question, arrest and detain people suspected of violating federal civil immigration law.

The Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, signed by Hochul on May 27, gave agencies with existing agreements 90 days to begin the process of ending them.

Under the law, covered agreements that remained in effect after Aug. 25 are considered void and unenforceable under New York law.

Why is New York suing the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office?

The Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office has maintained a 287(g) agreement with ICE since March 2020, according to the governor's and attorney general's offices.

After the new law was enacted, the attorney general's office contacted the sheriff's office seeking information about the status of the agreement. State officials said they did not receive confirmation that the agreement had been terminated or would be terminated by the Aug. 25 deadline.

On Aug. 19, the attorney general's office issued a formal investigative demand seeking documents showing what actions the sheriff's office had taken to end the agreement, according to the state.

State officials said they still have not received confirmation that the agreement was terminated.

"Compliance with the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act is not optional," Hochul said in a statement. "Today, we are taking action to ensure the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office performs the duties required of it under state law, because no one in New York State is above the law."

James said the lawsuit is intended to enforce the state's law.

"All law enforcement agencies are expected to uphold New York's laws," James said. "The Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office has been given every opportunity to follow the law, yet has chosen not to."

Rensselaer County is the only agency that has not indicated it will end its agreement

Of the 12 law enforcement agencies in New York that had 287(g) agreements before the new law took effect, the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office is the only one that has not indicated it intends to end its agreement, according to state officials.

The lawsuit asks the Rensselaer County Supreme Court to order the sheriff's office to exercise the termination provisions in its agreement with ICE and declare the agreement void and unenforceable under state law.

What is New York's Office of Immigrant Trust?

The lawsuit is the first legal action brought by the attorney general's newly established Office of Immigrant Trust.

The office was created to enforce New York laws limiting state and local involvement in federal civil immigration enforcement. It is authorized to investigate potential violations and bring civil lawsuits when appropriate.

Federal government also challenged New York's law

The U.S. Department of Justice filed a federal lawsuit in June challenging New York's Local Cops, Local Crimes Act.

Earlier this month, however, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York denied the federal government's request to block the state's ban on 287(g) agreements, allowing the Aug. 25 deadline to remain in effect.

text:
August 30, 2026 - New York — Immigrant families, workers, and legal assistance groups harmed by the Trump-Vance administration’s 75-country ban on immigrant visas filed an emergency motion to enforce Friday’s court order and judgment in CLINIC v. Rubio. The filing directly responds to reports that the U.S. State Department ordered a global “pause” on immigrant visa appointments, citing a training program as the reason after the court issued its order. On August 21, 2026, a federal court struck down the Trump-Vance administration’s blanket ban on immigrant visa processing for people from 75 countries and found the Secretary of State had no authority to “pause” or suspend visa processing.

“The August 21 ruling created an important path forward for families who have been waiting for their immigrant visa cases to move ahead,” said Adriana Coppola, supervising attorney of emerging issues at CLINIC. “CLINIC’s emergency motion is focused on ensuring that the court’s decision is implemented in a way that allows those cases to proceed fairly, individually, and with respect for the dignity of each person and the importance of family reunification.”

“The Administration cannot keep circumventing the legal system. This ban is unjust, and the court has agreed. We won’t let the Administration continue separating families and targeting our communities. It must resume processing visas and follow the law,” said Diana Konaté, Deputy Executive Director, African Communities Together.

“The court’s orders were crystal clear – the Trump-Vance administration’s Visa Ban is unlawful and cannot be enforced,” said Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward. “Yet the administration is egregiously and flagrantly ignoring a duly issued court order and enforcing unlawful policies that continue to inflict enormous harm on families and communities across the country. On behalf of our brave clients, we are asking the court to enforce its judgment and ensure that the government stops this abuse of power.”

“Families who have waited for months to be reunited with their loved ones continue to be separated across oceans as a result of the government refusing to abide by the court’s order and lift the blanket visa ban,” said Efrén C. Olivares, vice president of litigation & legal strategy at the National Immigration Law Center (NILC). “We continue to seek justice for our plaintiffs and have sought relief from the court to ensure the government complies with the order and judgment immediately.”

“The court was clear: the State Department cannot simply stop processing immigrant visas because it chooses to. Yet days after that ruling, the administration appears to be doing exactly that under a different name,” said Antionette Dozier, senior attorney, Western Center on Law & Poverty. “This blatant attempt to sidestep the law continues to keep families separated, disrupt lives, and leave people who have already endured months of uncertainty in limbo. A court order is not a suggestion. The administration must follow the law and resume processing these visas.”

“This administration’s seeming default is disorder and lawlessness, wherever that serves to hurt and exclude families of color,” said Baher Azmy, legal director of the Center for Constitutional Rights. “The executive branch shouldn’t have to be forced, again, to follow the law, yet we need additional judicial intervention to protect those families the administration seems determined to punish.”

“Legitimate global training programs are not rolled out in this manner,” said Sarah Wilson, partner & federal immigration litigation practice leader at Colombo & Hurd. “We are optimistic that the court will see this for what it is: blatant noncompliance with a thoughtful and well-reasoned court order.”

“The court’s decision made clear that the ban is unlawful and that the processing of visas for the families and workers impacted directly by the ban should proceed,” said Susan Welber, supervising attorney in the civil practice at The Legal Aid Society. “The Defendants’ outrageous attempt to thwart the processing of such visas worldwide smacks of animus and pretext.”

Plaintiffs include Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. (CLINIC), African Communities Together, and individuals whose lives were upended by the ban. They are represented by Democracy Forward, The National Immigration Law Center, The Legal Aid Society, the Western Center on Law & Poverty, the Center for Constitutional Rights, and Colombo & Hurd.

The lawsuit argued that the U.S. Department of State imposed an unlawful, discriminatory, nationality-based barrier to legal immigration that strips families and working people of the process guaranteed by law. The Trump-Vance administration baselessly cited “public charge” risk as its stated justification for the ban, after relentlessly and cruelly smearing immigrant communities, particularly communities of color.

The case is CLINIC v. Rubio, and the legal team at Democracy Forward includes Erez Reuveni, Catherine Carroll and Elena Goldstein.

text:
Friday’s ruling from the Third Circuit is the eighth from a federal appeals court to find the policy unlawful

August 30, 2026 - PHILADEPHIA — Another federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration’s new policy subjecting millions of immigrants to mandatory detention without access to bond hearings.

ICE recruitment graphic

Friday’s ruling from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit stems from a lawsuit brought by the American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of Pennsylvania, ACLU of New Jersey, and the law firm of Palladino, Isbell & Casazza, LLC. The case is Buele Morocho v. Warden Philadelphia FDC.

The Third Circuit decision joins similar rulings from seven other federal appeals courts and hundreds of district court judges in finding the policy unlawful.

For decades, immigrants in removal proceedings who were detained by the government have generally had the right to seek release by an immigration judge. In mid-2025, the Trump administration suddenly adopted a new radical reinterpretation of the immigration laws and declared that anyone who entered without inspection must be detained without access to bond.

Among those who were affected were people eligible for legal status, even those with long-pending immigration applications who have been waiting years due to administrative backlogs.

The following is reaction to today’s ruling:

“The courts have repeatedly and resoundingly rejected the Trump administration’s radical reinterpretation of our country’s detention laws. This ruling is another critical victory against the administration’s cruelty and disrespect for the rule of law. We are thrilled for our clients and their families,” said Michael Tan, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project.

“Even before the Trump administration began its campaign to detain every person it could round up, immigration detention was a cruel and unnecessary practice,” said Vanessa Stine, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of Pennsylvania. “But denying bond hearings to the individuals ICE detains is an alarming trend that is blatantly at odds with the plain text of the statute and the Constitution’s guarantee of due process. We applaud today’s decision and look forward to continuing the fight to end the Trump administration’s dangerous and unconstitutional targeting of immigrant communities.”

“This ruling underscores that this administration cannot make up its own rules in order to lock up huge numbers of people without a bond hearing,” said Farrin Anello, senior counsel for the ACLU of New Jersey. “We applaud the court’s careful and painstaking analysis of the statutes in question and its conclusion that the government must follow the plain language of the law and the Constitution in order to take away someone’s freedom. Today is a win for immigrants’ rights and the rule of law.”

“Within the Third Circuit, this decision puts an end to a year-long campaign by the administration to indefinitely detain human beings without due process. We feel incredibly fortunate to have co-counseled with this legal team on this case," said Christopher M. Casazza, attorney with Palladino, Isbell & Casazza, LLC.

title: You Could Be Next: Trump's Gestapo Tactics Are Getting Worse | Common Dreams
description:
As he loses power and popularity — and faces mounting resistance abroad and at home — Trump is enlarging his police state.
His regime is having ever more people arrested, imprisoned, and deported without any judge or jury deciding they did anything wrong.
Trump’s police state not only continues, but it is growing larger by the day.
The Trump regime has unilaterally revoked temporary protected status and claims the ankle monitors are necessary to track people whom it may want to deport at some point.
Finally, the Trump regime is imprisoning Americans who demonstrate against its police state.
text:
Imagine living in a country that can arrest and imprison you whenever it wants, without any judge or jury deciding you did anything wrong. It can call you a “domestic terrorist” and put you in prison for life. It can even execute you on the basis of nothing more than its own decision that you’re dangerous.

Well, I have bad news for you. You’re living in that country right now.

As he loses power and popularity — and faces mounting resistance abroad and at home — Trump is enlarging his police state.

His regime is having ever more people arrested, imprisoned, and deported without any judge or jury deciding they did anything wrong. It’s using racial profiling in deciding whom to target. It’s making warrantless searches and seizures of people, their cars, and their homes. All of this violates the US Constitution.

Trump’s police state not only continues, but it is growing larger by the day.

According to a new analysis by The New York Times, the regime’s surge in immigration arrests this summer has swept up thousands of people, most of whom have not been charged with or convicted of a crime (less than 4 percent had a past violent criminal conviction).

Those being arrested, imprisoned, and potentially deported include some married to US citizens, others who entered the US legally and are pursuing asylum claims, and some who came here with temporary legal status that the Trump regime has decided to revoke.

In other words, they were all here legally.

If you have temporary protected status because you escaped from inhumane conditions in another country, ICE might now summon you to an ICE office and put a monitor around your ankle — even if you have no criminal history and are in full compliance with your immigration status. The Trump regime has unilaterally revoked temporary protected status and claims the ankle monitors are necessary to track people whom it may want to deport at some point.

You’re not even safe if you’re a US citizen born in America. ProPublica has found that more than 170 US citizens have been wrongfully detained by ICE agents in raids and protests over a recent nine-month span. It described cases involving alleged force and multiday detention without access to counsel or communication.

Some estimates put the number of US citizens subjected to ICE as much higher, but there’s no way of knowing because there’s no legal process for filtering out and protecting American citizens, just as there’s no legal process for protecting anyone else who’s here legally. Trump’s police state is extrajudicial, and it’s being done in secret.

You might even be murdered, without a trial finding you guilty of anything. In addition to Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota last January, ICE agents have murdered two others just this summer.

One was Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, murdered by ICE in Houston on July 7, 2026. Salgado Araujo had lived in the US for decades. ICE agents pursued him in unmarked cars and shot him while he was driving a work crew to a job site. The Department of Homeland Security claims Salgado Araujo tried to use his vehicle as a weapon against an officer, but witnesses dispute this account.

The other was Johan Sebastian Durán Guerrero, murdered by ICE on July 13, 2026, in Biddeford, Maine. Durán Guerrero was a 25-year-old immigrant from Colombia. Agents pursued him while he was driving to work. The Department of Homeland Security claims its agent feared for public safety as Durán Guerrero tried to drive away, but elected officials and family members dispute this account, noting that Durán Guerrero was not an intended target of the immigration operation.

None of these murders has been fully investigated.

You might also be murdered without a trial if you happen to be on a vessel off Latin America’s Caribbean coast or in the eastern Pacific Ocean. A mere accusation of drug trafficking is enough to kill you, without any evidence presented before any court of law or neutral magistrate.

Historians looking back on this shameful period will wonder how this was allowed.

The US military announced Monday that it had again carried out a strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people it accused of trafficking drugs — bringing the overall death toll to 223 people killed in 67 strikes during the nearly yearlong US campaign of bombing boats alleged to be smuggling drugs.

Finally, the Trump regime is imprisoning Americans who demonstrate against its police state.

In June, in two federal courts sentenced nine people who protested outside an immigrant detention facility in Texas to 30 to 100 years in prison, after the regime accused them of being members of Antifa. During the protest, a police officer was shot; he survived.

Those sentences are longer than the harshest sentence handed down to any of the convicted rioters in the January 6 attack on the US Capitol in 2021 (all of whom have since received pardons or commutations from Trump).

These cases are the first to incorporate new guidance from the regime that classifies Antifa as a “domestic terrorist organization.” That’s despite the fact that Antifa is a decentralized movement rather than a single organization and that there is no federal charge of domestic terrorism under existing US law.

I want to make three concluding points about all this.

First, Trump’s police state not only continues, but it is growing larger by the day. Kristi Noem’s replacement as secretary of homeland security, Markwayne Mullin, along with his boss in the White House, Stephen Miller, and the secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth, have more money, manpower, and firepower than ever. They are ramping up all of their extrajudicial arrests, detentions, deportations, and murders.

The only difference between last year and now is they’re no longer announcing what they’re doing with fanfare and braggadocio, because the American public has grown wary of it.

Second, none of us is safe from this because the arrests, installations of ankle bracelets, imprisonments, deportations, and murders are made without any judge, jury, or neutral party deciding that the assumptions on which they’re based are adequate and truthful.

Not even “domestic terrorism” arrests and lengthy prison sentences necessitate judicial inquiry into what exactly is meant by “domestic terrorism” and whether defendants have done anything to justify that appellation.

Finally, this growing menace is cruel, inhumane, and likely unconstitutional. It is causing hundreds of thousands of families in our country extreme mental distress; many people are not leaving their homes for fear of being arrested or worse. It is likely chilling First Amendment rights to speak up and protest against these atrocities.

title: Documents leaked by Trump official to bolster a conspiracy show 'absolutely nothing'
description:
Rogers, who denied this claim, then published the files herself, claiming officials inside the center “betrayed their stated mission”.
The files included a 2022 GEC report on “gendered disinformation”, a flashpoint in the culture wars.
The center was abolished in 2025, and what remained of its work scattered across the state department.
The question raised by the files leaked this month is narrower, however: whether they show the GEC itself ran a domestic censorship operation.
Contacted for comment, the state department declined to directly address questions about the documents released by Rogers, the influencer proposal, the department’s current foreign influence programs and whether other regions are being targeted as well.
text:
A botched leak of purportedly explosive government files to a prominent conservative online personality was supposed to offer proof of what the Trump administration and its allies have long alleged: that a little-known office inside the US state department, created to fight foreign propaganda, had secretly become a tool for domestic censorship.

Two former high-ranking officials at the Global Engagement Center (GEC), a target of Republican ire that lost its funding in 2024 and was disbanded after Donald Trump’s return to office in 2025, say the documents show nothing of the kind.

Instead, they argue, the files are a symptom of a protracted and bitter political fight over an office that spent nearly a decade tracking and countering foreign influence operations, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.

And the state department is now resuming some of this work in other parts of its operation, including plans – laid out in a proposal reviewed by the Guardian – to pay social media influencers across south-east Asia as part of an $11m campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.

Sarah Rogers, the state department’s undersecretary for public diplomacy, provided the so-called “GEC files” to Jennica Pounds, a rightwing online data analyst known as DataRepublican – only for Pounds to claim earlier this month she was leaked the documents as part of a bid to “entrap” her.

Rogers, who denied this claim, then published the files herself, claiming officials inside the center “betrayed their stated mission”. The files included a 2022 GEC report on “gendered disinformation”, a flashpoint in the culture wars.

“These guys have consistently misrepresented what the GEC did, and this was a great example of that,” said Daniel Kimmage, who served as the center’s principal deputy coordinator and acting coordinator from its founding in 2017 until its complete dissolution in 2025. His own congressional testimony was included in the leaked files.

Kimmage and Carrie Goux, a Joe Biden appointee and the center’s former acting deputy coordinator, say nothing in the material shows the GEC, whose mandate was explicitly foreign-facing, ever turned its tools on Americans.

“If the smoking gun was a gendered disinformation report, that feels like they came up short,” Goux said. “There seems to be absolutely nothing here.”

Weaponization

The dispute is the latest chapter in a years-long campaign by conservatives to portray the GEC as part of a broader effort by the US government and technology companies to suppress rightwing speech.

Republican congressmen including Michael McCaul, former chair of the House foreign affairs committee, argued in a July 2024 letter that the GEC was “at best indifferent to, and at worst complicit in” stretching the definition of disinformation to “censor” conservative speech in the US.

Trump’s return to the presidency drew this view into the heart of the federal government. The center was abolished in 2025, and what remained of its work scattered across the state department.

Much of that Republican-led campaign centered on how the GEC had funded the Global Disinformation Index (GDI), a UK-based non-profit that rates media outlets by how likely they are to spread disinformation, to help monitor propaganda in Asia. But in 2022 the GDI separately published its own study of the US media market that rated several conservative outlets, including Newsmax, One America News and the New York Post, as high-risk – a finding its critics have cited ever since as evidence that a foreign-facing office had funded a group meddling in domestic politics.

The question raised by the files leaked this month is narrower, however: whether they show the GEC itself ran a domestic censorship operation. Kimmage and Goux insist they do not.

Kimmage said his own congressional testimony, which Rogers included in the leak, had been selectively read. “If you look at the transcript, [the question was], ‘Does GEC take positions on US outlets?’ And I said, ‘No, it didn’t,’” he said.

Rogers “tried to twist that into something that it wasn’t”, according to Kimmage. “For people who talk a lot about weaponization of government, this seems a lot closer to the weaponization of government and psy-opping of the American people than anything that the emails from the Global Engagement Center show.”

‘False’ allegations

Pounds, the rightwing analyst, is not a neutral bystander. Days after the documents were released, she disclosed that she had been quietly working since July as a special government employee for the defense department.

On Friday, Pounds released a database to track US citizens in the Democratic Socialists of America. The Pentagon did not respond when asked whether the database is included in her scope of government work.

Both former senior officials, Kimmage and Goux, draw a sharp line between the accusations made by critics of the GEC and what the center actually did. “We were not ever looking at Americans,” Goux said. “We were looking at the foreign actors and what their [tactics, techniques and procedures] … are doing overseas.”

The GEC “did what its congressional mandate charged it to do, which is to fight foreign [misinformation and] disinformation”, added Kimmage. “This allegation that it’s censoring Americans is false.”

During its almost decade-long existence, the center published eight detailed public reports on Russian and Chinese information operations and ran four major exposures of Russian disinformation campaigns – in Latin America, Africa and Moldova, and on the Kremlin-linked network RT.

Its largest such operation traced a Kremlin-backed effort called the “African Initiative”, which the center said had recruited local journalists, bloggers and public figures to spread conspiracy theories about US-funded health programs across the continent.

In January 2024, the GEC helped broker an international pact on countering foreign state disinformation that eventually drew more than two dozen government signatories, among them Moldova, Spain, Estonia, Poland and Finland – a framework its backers hoped other countries would use to build their own version of the office.

A 2022 inspector general review found the GEC “generally effective” at supporting counter-disinformation programs overall, while flagging weaknesses in its internal controls, contractor oversight and strategic planning. That record was enough to sustain bipartisan support: senators Rob Portman, a Republican, and Chris Murphy, a Democrat, repeatedly pushed to fund and strengthen the center, and its authorization survived multiple renewal fights before House Republicans, increasingly focused on the domestic-speech question, declined to extend it again in 2024.

That mandate cost roughly $61m per year. The GEC employed about 120 people before Congress declined to reauthorize it, letting the office lapse at the end of 2024. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, later folded what remained of its work into a new counter foreign information manipulation and interference office, framing the closure as an end to wasteful, censorious government overreach.

Trust exercise

Now, less than a year after the GEC shut down, a proposal reviewed by the Guardian shows the state department preparing to pay up to 30 online influencers across 11 countries in south-east Asia $2,500 apiece as part of an $11m, multi-year campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.

The project, which would be operated by the US Mission to USEAN, has three parts: a $5m messaging campaign, a $3m program training influencers and journalists to counter Chinese propaganda, and a $3m trip bringing about 180 participants to studios in Washington and Houston “for intensive collaboration, studio production and first-hand engagement with US institutions and creators”.

The proposal’s planning materials describe the ideal recruit as starting from a “welcoming” position of what one document calls the “rejecting-affirming continuum”: someone not yet sold on the US, but not hostile either. As participants move through the accelerator, the materials say, exposure to evidence of US commitment in the region and training in spotting propaganda from China (which has reportedly invested billions of dollars in disinformation efforts globally) is meant to carry them toward the “affirming” end of that scale, publicly backing closer ties with Washington on trade, tech standards and the South China Sea.

The document cited the rightwing analyst and new Pentagon special government employee, Jennica Pounds, the DataRepublican, as an ideal model to seek out in other recruits abroad.

Contacted for comment, the state department declined to directly address questions about the documents released by Rogers, the influencer proposal, the department’s current foreign influence programs and whether other regions are being targeted as well.

A state department official said: “Undersecretary Rogers has been clear that the department will continue to confront censorship, anti-American propaganda and coercive influence directly while demonstrating the enduring advantages of freedom, accountability and open communication.”

Meanwhile, the office of policy, planning and resources for public diplomacy (R/PPR) was separately shopping for commercial help with a similar mission this spring. A government filing from May 2026 shows the R/PPR requesting information from vendors on software that can mine open-source data, map “adversarial propaganda influence networks” and detect deepfakes.

That apparent contradiction is not lost on the GEC’s former staff.

“Are they trying to re-create it? Probably,” Goux said. “But now they’re spending a lot more tax dollars doing that, trying to get contractors to do some of the stuff that we were doing.”

Goux put the broader cost in plainer terms still. “The US has lost their seat at the table to do that, and that’s unfortunate,” she said. “I hope we can gain it back, but we’re losing trust too, and that’s significant.”

text:
DAKAR, Senegal — The United States on Saturday deported dozens of people to the Central African Republic, including an Afghan whose brothers collaborated with the U.S. military, his lawyer and an advocacy group said.

The Afghan man, who is in his early twenties, was granted protection against deportation to Afghanistan by a U.S. judge due to fears of persecution by the Taliban, his lawyer Alma David said.

His family in Afghanistan had received threats from the Taliban because of the work performed by the brothers in support of the U.S. military, according to court documents seen by The Associated Press.

One of the Afghan man's brothers lives in the United States and served in the Afghan National Army, which collaborated with the U.S military before the Taliban seized power in 2021, David said.

Another one of his brothers was a pilot trained by the U.S. and was killed by the Taliban, she added.

The deportation flight which landed in Central African Republic's capital Bangui on Saturday, included 12 Afghans and eight Iranians, as well as several people from Nepal and Nicaragua, said Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.

Under a series of often secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to two dozen countries that aren't their own as it pushes ahead with its immigration crackdown, advocates say. Immigration lawyers say the practice is being used as a legal loophole to indirectly return some asylum seekers to countries they fled. The flight on Saturday is the second to the Central African Republic since June, which carried two dozen migrants, including an Iranian woman facing persecution in her home country.

The Trump administration sold MPP as a way to thwart people with fraudulent claims from easily entering the U.S.
text:
Spotlight PA is an independent, nonpartisan, and nonprofit newsroom producing investigative and public-service journalism that holds power to account and drives positive change in Pennsylvania. Sign up for our free newsletters.

HARRISBURG — Earlier this spring, with no public notice, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro made an unconventional hire: a senior advisor to help him deal with the Trump administration.

Jennifer Higgins, a longtime federal immigration official based in Washington, D.C., was brought on to help Shapiro and state agencies under his jurisdiction map out responses to some of the president’s targeted attacks on Democrat-led states — notably, funding cuts and demands for sensitive or proprietary information.

Higgins is being paid by the hour — an unusual arrangement for a gubernatorial staffer, and one that Shapiro’s office could not immediately explain. State payroll records show she is paid $89 per hour, and Shapiro officials said she works full-time, putting her annual salary at roughly $185,000.

The administration defended hiring Higgins, even though Pennsylvania already spends tens of thousands of taxpayer dollars every year for a federal government liaison.

The governor’s office employs a full-time lobbyist in Washington, D.C., who is paid $177,507 annually. And in theory, Pennsylvania’s two senators act as the state’s de facto protectors in the nation’s capital and run interference with the White House when problems arise.

But Shapiro spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky explained in an emailed statement that an additional person was needed because “the Trump administration’s relentless attacks on the rights and freedoms of Pennsylvanians are reaching into every corner of our Commonwealth.”

Higgins, Lapowsky said, brings “deep expertise and invaluable perspective helping protect Pennsylvanians during this critical moment.” (Higgins did not respond to Spotlight PA’s request to speak with her directly.)

Still, Higgins’ expertise is in the immigration sphere, where she has spent nearly the entirety of her career. The governor’s office acknowledged that Higgins is not directly advising Shapiro on immigration issues, but is part of a larger group of policy officials, lawyers, and others who provide the governor with information on that and other issues facing the state.

Asked for an example of Higgins’ work, Lapowsky said she helped coordinate Shapiro’s response to a Trump administration demand that states turn over commercial driver's license records containing personal information. Trump officials have pointed, among other things, to crashes involving noncitizen drivers as one reason for the crackdown and have threatened to withhold federal funding if states do not comply.

In August, Shapiro joined a coalition of state attorneys general suing the federal government over the subpoena.

It’s true that, since reclaiming the White House in 2024, President Donald Trump has used the levers of the federal government to punish blue states.

The administration admitted in a federal court filing this summer that it recommended scrapping billions in grants for clean-energy projects based solely on those states’ “political identity,” and whether Trump won the vote in those places in the 2024 election.

Earlier this year, Trump attempted to freeze billions in childcare and social assistance for five Democratic-led states — he had initiated the move following the federal fraud probe involving Minnesota’s social services network — which he later abandoned.

And Politico reported last month that Trump overruled his own emergency management agency to deny federal relief funds to four Democratic-led states.

For his part, Shapiro often talks about how his administration has sued Trump dozens of times to challenge the loss of federal funding. Those suits involve a range of initiatives, from education to natural disasters. The governor’s office also noted that unlike in other states, where attorneys general are handling litigation against Trump, Shapiro’s lawyers are taking on that work in Pennsylvania. Attorney General Dave Sunday, a Republican, has not entered the commonwealth into any lawsuit against the president or his administration.

Many of those suits predate Higgins’ arrival, and were handled by attorneys already on Shapiro’s staff. But the volume of attacks coming from Washington, Lapowsky said, combined with the range and breadth of policies and issues being targeted, necessitated another person to help coordinate plans to respond.

Immigration leadership

Higgins’ role in the Shapiro administration differs significantly from the work that has defined her career.

She started as an immigration officer in the early 2000s, but quickly moved into leadership roles within the federal office that handles asylum applications and screenings and adjudicates refugee applications, according to an online biography.

Shortly after Trump was elected to a first term in 2016, Higgins became the office’s associate director. Some rights groups have highlighted that part of her bio, since she held a leadership position during the implementation of one of the federal government’s most controversial immigration programs.

Officially called the Migrant Protection Protocols (MPP), but better known as Remain in Mexico, the program went into effect in early 2019. It required asylum seekers along the southern border to return to cities in Mexico, many of which are dangerous, while waiting for their immigration cases to be heard in the courts. Previously, those people were allowed to stay in the United States during that waiting period.

The Trump administration sold MPP as a way to thwart people with fraudulent claims from easily entering the U.S. But human rights and immigration groups, as well as multiple news organizations, extensively documented how migrants sent to Mexican border towns faced extreme danger, including kidnapping, assault, and rape. Tent camps were set up to house some of the asylum seekers, but living conditions were squalid, with no running water or electricity.

Human rights groups also noted that access to legal representation was fraught with obstacles, and resulted in higher numbers of cases being denied, sometimes just because migrants did not receive timely notices of their hearings or could not safely reach ports of entry into the country to be present for such hearings.

The office where Higgins held a senior leadership role at the time — the Refugee, Asylum and International Operations Directorate (RAIO) inside the U.S. Department of Homeland Security — was part of the larger apparatus tasked with the MPP’s rollout. Higgins’ level of involvement in the program’s operations is not clear, as the office’s work is subject to high levels of confidentiality. But the office she helped oversee is responsible for, among other duties, conducting asylum screenings and applications, according to its website. Its employees would have been at the front lines of the program’s implementation.

President Joe Biden ended the Remain in Mexico program after defeating Trump in 2020. Since retaking the White House, Trump officials have attempted to revive it but have been blocked by the courts.

During Biden’s presidency, Higgins continued to rise. She became acting chief of staff to then-U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, and within a year was appointed acting director of the department’s vast agency that oversees the legal U.S. immigration system.

Shortly after Trump started his second term, she was replaced.

text:
(The Hill) — Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is planning to spend up to $2 million on robot “dogs” to assist its agents’ operations, according to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funding document.

A funding document posted to DHS’s Acquisition Planning Forecast System on Thursday said the agency could spend between $1 million and $2 million on Boston Dynamics’ “Spot” robot and accessories.

A senior DHS official confirmed the plans to NBC News and told the outlet that the robots will not be used to make arrests. The Hill has reached out to ICE for comment.

The technology is already in use by several law enforcement agencies, including the Los Angeles and New York police departments. The U.S. Secret Service also previously used the robotic dogs to secure President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago home in 2024.

These robots are equipped with cameras and sensors that can detect vibration, gas and radiation, according to Boston Dynamics.

In the government funding notice description, the agency said these robots will allow for “inspection, situational awareness, and hazard assessment in environments that may pose risks to personnel.”

“This capability helps improve officer safety, supports informed operational decision-making, and enhances DHS’s ability to respond to incidents involving dangerous, confined, unstable, or difficult-to-access areas,” the notice states.

Boston Dynamics said in its ethics statement that it “will not authorize nor partner with those who wish to use our robots as weapons or autonomous targeting systems.”

“If our products are being used for harm, we will take appropriate measures to mitigate that misuse,” the company continued.

This new proposal follows the agency’s controversial decision earlier this month to purchase as much as $20 million worth of electric shock gloves for officers to wear during immigration operations. White House border czar Tom Homan defended the move against criticism, arguing the gloves would prevent agents from needing to resort to deadly force.

“In America, free speech doesn’t just belong to the people who say things the government agrees with,” FIRE attorney Conor Fitzpatrick said in a statement Friday.

text:
The Trump administration violated the Constitution when it moved to deport or rescind visas from international students who spoke up for Palestinian rights and criticized Israel's genocide in Gaza, a federal judge ruled on Friday.

Northern District of California Judge Noël Wise, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, said that the administration's actions violated both the First Amendment of the Constitution protecting free speech and the Fifth Amendment ensuring due process.

"Stated plainly, in the United States, freedom of speech belongs to the people. It is not the government’s to take," Wise wrote.

Mahmoud Khalil, a Columbia University student who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement early in the second Trump administration despite holding a green card, celebrated the ruling on Saturday.

"A federal judge just ruled that the Trump admin's use of immigration law to deport me and other noncitizen students for pro-Palestinian speech is unconstitutional. No one should fear speaking up for Palestine," Khalil wrote on social media.

The Council on American-Islamic Relations also welcomed the decision in a statement on Saturday:

This ruling reaffirms a fundamental American principle that the government cannot deport people simply because it dislikes their political views. Students do not surrender their constitutional rights at the classroom door, and international students do not surrender their freedom of expression when they come to study in the United States. Criticizing the policies of a foreign government, including the genocidal government of Israel, is protected political speech.

The lawsuit was brought by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) in August 2025 on behalf of The Stanford Daily, Stanford University's student newspaper, and an anonymous female plaintiff. The newspaper argued that student reporters on visas refrained from covering pro-Palestinian protests on campus out of fear of being deported, while the Jane Doe was a noncitizen who had spoken out on behalf of Palestine and now was worried about government retaliation.

"The reporters in our newsroom shouldn’t have to fear that writing a story will result in their deportation. Today’s victory means they won’t have to," the paper's editor-in-chief George Porteous wrote on social media on Friday.

In particular, the lawsuit challenged two provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act that Secretary of State Marco Rubio used to justify seeking the deportations of Khalil, Columbia student Moshen Mahdawi, and Tufts University student Rümeysa Öztürk. The first allows the secretary of state to deport a noncitizen for speech if the secretary “personally determines” the speech “compromises a compelling foreign policy interest.” The second allows the secretary to revoke visas entirely at their own discretion.

Wise agreed that the provisions violated the Constitution and offered a rousing defense of free speech.

“In the United States, free speech, including the freedom to criticize the government and its leaders, is not a sign of our democracy’s fragility. It is evidence of its strength," she wrote. "That strength is diminished when members of our society—citizens and noncitizens alike—must self-censor and ‘behave’ or suffer the government’s retaliation.”

FIRE said the decision was the "first in the country to squarely rule on the constitutionality of these statutes" and that it would "reverberate in similar proceedings around the country."

“In America, free speech doesn’t just belong to the people who say things the government agrees with,” FIRE attorney Conor Fitzpatrick said in a statement Friday. “Today’s ruling proves that free speech isn’t a privilege, but the inalienable right of every man, woman, and child.”

text:
The crisis that unfolded this summer in Ceuta [a Spanish enclave located in Morocco] was marked by the sudden arrival of 72,000 people on European soil, rekindling fears surrounding immigration. Yet the next major turning point in the continent's migration policy will not be what many expect. While the public debate has centered on how to curb immigration, the main question soon facing European governments will be how to attract foreign workers, whom their economies will need. In fact, that shift has already begun.

Italy is perhaps the most striking example of this shift. In June 2022, Giorgia Meloni, who was still in the opposition at the time (she became prime minister in October), traveled to Andalusia to support the far-right Spanish Vox candidate, denouncing "mass immigration" and calling for secure borders. Nine months later, in Cutro [Calabria], after the deaths of ninety-four people in the Mediterranean, she justified the reinstatement of the decreto flussi [decree regulating migratory flows] by citing the needs of the Italian "productive world." The measure was set to allow for the arrival of 452,000 foreign workers between 2023 and 2025, and nearly 500,000 more between 2026 and 2028. Since Meloni has been in power, immigration to the Peninsula has increased by more than 10%.

Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban (in office from 2010 to 2026) followed a similar path, albeit with even less publicity. Although he made the fight against immigration one of the pillars of his power, he largely opened his country to so-called "guest workers." According to Eurostat, the number of new residence permits issued there rose from 20,751 in 2015 to 87,624 in 2024. When adjusted for population, that is higher than the European average and nearly double the level in France.

As for the Social Democratic government in Denmark, generally praised by the far right for its "tough and dissuasive migration policy," it issued, on average, three times more residence permits than France in 2024 – amounting to 1.43% of its population, or 86,000 new immigrants (for a population of six million), with 50% of them coming from countries outside the OECD [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development]. The only reduction in migration flows in Denmark concerned those related to asylum, which has been almost entirely eliminated (11,000 refugees in 2015, 875 in 2025). A strange interpretation of social democracy!

text:
The Trump administration violated the Constitution when it revoked visas and sought to detain noncitizen students for expressing dissent, particularly while condemning Israel’s actions in Gaza, a federal judge in California ruled Friday.

U.S. District Judge Noël Wise ruled that Secretary of State Marco Rubio violated the First Amendment and the Fifth Amendment when he invoked the Immigration and Nationality Act to cancel student visas and initiate deportation proceedings. Rubio vowed in March 2025 to crack down on pro-Palestinian international students, saying in a news conference at the time, “Every time I find one of these lunatics, I take away their visa.”

Tensions escalated last year after federal immigration authorities detained Mahmoud Khalil, a student protest leader at Columbia University, and Rümeysa Öztürk, a doctoral student at Tufts University who wrote an opinion piece for the student newspaper. Those arrests and others spurred criticism from free-speech advocacy organizations.

Stanford University’s student-run newspaper and an unnamed female student with an F-1 visa sued Rubio in August 2025, arguing that his policy was stifling free speech on college campuses. The Stanford Daily said in the lawsuit that international students were afraid to write news stories or opinion pieces in fear of having their visas revoked.

Trending

In her 90-page ruling Friday, Wise said “freedom of speech belongs to the people. It is not the government’s to take.” She said President Donald Trump’s administration has followed a pattern of targeting dissent, including pro-Palestinian support, critiques of conservative political activist Charlie Kirk after he was fatally shot, and opinions about the Iran war.

“This downward spiral is antithetical to our Constitution that recognizes our right to speak freely,” wrote Wise, a Joe Biden appointee. “Here you can simultaneously hate the content of a person’s speech and love the country that cherishes the freedom to allow it. Zealous protection of our Constitutional right to free speech is a provocative demonstration of our country’s powerful lack of fear.”

The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday on Wise’s ruling.

The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a civil rights organization that helped litigate the case, said in a statement that Wise’s ruling “proves that free speech isn’t a privilege, but the inalienable right of every man, woman, and child.”

While Wise’s ruling found the Trump administration’s actions to be unconstitutional, she stopped short of ordering the government to cease its deportation threats because only the Supreme Court has the authority to block that provision.

title: Only legal assistance and public exposure can save Katya - BYSOL
description:
Katya Bartko applied for asylum in the United States because of political persecution in Belarus.
Her partner Dmitry is asking for help to free her from detention with the assistance of lawyers and prevent her deportation to Belarus.
In March 2022, Katya legally entered the United States on a student visa, and in February 2023 she applied for asylum.
Only legal assistance and public exposure can save her.
But legal protection in the United States involves enormous costs for me.
text:
Katya Bartko applied for asylum in the United States because of political persecution in Belarus. As a result of a wrongful arrest, she ended up in an immigration detention centre, without the life-saving medication she needs, and came within a hair's breadth of death. Her partner Dmitry is asking for help to free her from detention with the assistance of lawyers and prevent her deportation to Belarus.

My name is Dmitry. I am appealing to everyone who cares for help on behalf of and with the permission of my girlfriend, Katerina Bartko, because she is physically unable to do so herself right now: she is in ICE immigration detention in Kansas, USA. I am her partner and officially authorized representative for medical and legal matters.

Katya is Belarusian, 33 years old, and originally from Hlybokaye. In 2020, during the presidential “campaign,” she worked as a teacher and refused to take her students to early voting for pro-government candidates, for which she was punished by the school administration. She took part in the peaceful marches of 2020 and supported the Belarusian democratic movement, and after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, she openly published anti-war materials.

Her loved ones were persecuted for the same reasons. After the outbreak of the war, her former partner helped document the movement of Russian military equipment, for which he was convicted. Photographs from peaceful marches were used as evidence in his case – and Katya was next to him in every one of them.

The authorities became interested in her. They investigated where Katya lived, who her friends and relatives were, and which social media accounts and names she used. Pro-government channels published photographs of the two of them together along with his forced confession video. And in October 2022, people came looking for Katya at her parents' home.

In March 2022, Katya legally entered the United States on a student visa, and in February 2023 she applied for asylum. She was waiting her turn, like thousands of Belarusians. But in June 2026, following a wrongful arrest over a minor case – subsequently dismissed for lack of guilt, with no conviction or criminal record – she ended up in ICE detention.

And here, a legal problem turned into a threat to her life. Katya's thyroid gland was removed because of cancer. To function normally, she needs to take hormones and calcium every day for the rest of her life – without them, her body begins to fail within days.

In detention, continuity of her treatment was disrupted: during the first four days, she was taken to hospital by ambulance three times, one of these hospitalizations involving critically dangerous, life-threatening readings. Her medication was then taken away – and for almost three weeks, she was given nothing. According to the latest available results, Katya's TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone, which is produced by the thyroid gland or taken in tablet form by a person without a thyroid gland, and is necessary for the body's functioning) is 33 times above the normal level. She is at risk of myxedema coma, a condition with a mortality rate of 25–60%.

She was denied release on bail on a single formal ground: over the previous years, she had moved between states several times, and this was deemed a “flight risk” for failing to appear at hearings.

Only legal assistance and public exposure can save her. I don't sleep at night. I write to senators, oversight bodies, and journalists. Sometimes I feel like giving up. But then I remember that public exposure has already worked once – after media reports, she began receiving the medication she had been without for three weeks – and I keep going.

But legal protection in the United States involves enormous costs for me. That is why I am asking for your help. Each legal action is billed separately: preparing a federal lawsuit demanding immediate treatment or release, the work of immigration lawyers, every motion, every hearing.

Immigration court proceedings and legal representation in her asylum case are the most important things right now, so that she can be released from detention and not deported to Belarus.

What do I feel? Fear – every day that I won't make it in time. The woman I love, who beat cancer, is behind bars not for a crime, but because she asked for protection – on the brink between life and death.

If you are Belarusian, you know why Katya cannot return home. If you are simply a person who cares – imagine that someone close to you became seriously ill in a foreign country, behind bars, without medication. Help me get Katya to her asylum hearing alive.

Every donation will bring Katya closer to being saved!

text:
The United States has deported 12 Afghan nationals to the Central African Republic. Among them is a young Afghan man whom a US judge had previously protected from deportation to Afghanistan because of fears he could face persecution by the Taliban.

The deportation flight landed Saturday in Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, carrying 12 Afghans and eight Iranians, along with several people from Nepal and Nicaragua, according to Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.

The Afghan man, who is in his early 20s, had been granted protection from removal to Afghanistan by a US immigration judge because of concerns that he could face persecution by the Taliban, his lawyer, Alma David, said.

His family in Afghanistan had received threats from the Taliban because of his brothers’ involvement in supporting the US military, according to court documents reviewed by The Associated Press.

One of his brothers lives in the United States and served in the former Afghan National Army, which worked alongside US forces before the Taliban seized control of Afghanistan in 2021, David said.

Another brother was a US-trained pilot who was later killed by the Taliban, she said. The New York Times, which identified the deported man only as Khalil, reported that his sister and father also worked alongside US forces.

AfghanEvac, a US-based organization that assists Afghan allies, as well as the American Civil Liberties Union and Human Rights First, also confirmed the man’s deportation.

Human Rights First said Saturday’s flight was the third US deportation flight to the Central African Republic this year.

The Trump administration has sent thousands of people to third countries with which they have no ties under a series of agreements as it pursues a broader immigration crackdown.

The US State Department advises Americans not to travel to the Central African Republic for any reason, citing risks including unrest, crime, kidnapping, health threats and terrorism.

text:
The remains of 19 dead migrants, including children, were found in the Arizona desert near the U.S.-Mexico border last month, a two-year record, according to data from the Pima County Office of the Medical Examiner and the advocacy group Humane Borders.

Among the deceased, five appeared to have been dead for less than a day and two had been dead for less than a week when they were found.

“This is a persistent and perennial problem, it's not just a July 2026 problem,” Brad Jones, a political science professor at the UC Davis Global Migration Center and a Humane Borders board member, told the Arizona Daily Star.

“It does ebb and flow, but it never goes away,” he said. “We’ve never had a period of zero recovered remains” since Humane Borders was founded in 2000, acording to Jones.

The record number of deaths, likely an undercount, is all the more striking because border crossings have plunged overall since Donald Trump took office and tightened a variety of immigration policies, including effectively cutting off all asylum claims and restricting entries at the southern border.

There were nearly 10 times fewer encounters between Border Patrol agents and migrants in July 2026 than during the same month in 2024, the final full year of Joe Biden’s administration.

As The Independent has reported, the U.S. has long pursued a strategy of “prevention through deference,” using military-style security infrastructure such as walls and barbed wire at popular points of entry to push migrants into remote rural areas spanning the lengthy U.S.-Mexico border, in the hopes that the danger of the crossing will prevent future migration.

Critics argue that undocumented immigration into the U.S. is often driven by life-or-death factors and migrants will make the journey regardless of what kind of barriers are in their way, exposing already-vulnerable people to injury and death along the mountains, rivers and deserts of the borderlands.

The Trump administration has continued to fortify the border, thanks in part to a $46 billion infusion of funds from Congress to continue building its signature border wall, which was largely paused during the Biden administration.

Border construction efforts have continued across Arizona, New Mexico and Texas, despite opposition from indigenous tribes, environmental advocates and park boosters, who have been particularly incensed by a plan to add new border security infrastructure within Big Bend National Park, an area that’s not a high-traffic illegal immigration zone.

In addition to adding new physical barriers at the border, the Trump administration has sought massive changes to the legal regime along the frontier.

The White House has argued migration into the U.S. constitutes an invasion and gives the administration the power to remove undocumented border crossers without giving them a chance to seek asylum, a right which is protected under U.S. and human rights law. Lower courts have blocked the policy, though the Trump administration is seeking a Supreme Court appeal.

The administration has also revoked temporary protected status rights for people from a variety of nations, policies which had given tens of thousands of immigrants from unstable regions reprieve from deportation.

Last year, 32 people died in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody, the most deaths in more than two decades.

text:
British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos was deported to the United Kingdom after his arrest by American immigration authorities, U.S. officials said Saturday.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Yiannopoulos was returned to his home country Friday after being accused of overstaying after entering the U.S. legally in May 2019. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal July 22 after he failed to show up for an immigration hearing, a Homeland Security spokesperson said.

Yiannopoulos was arrested Thursday at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Louisiana and detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement.

Yiannopoulos and his representatives did not respond to requests for comment, and he has not posted on the social platform X since Thursday.

Yiannopoulos backed President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown

Yiannopoulos is a well-known champion of conservative causes and has frequently taken provocative public positions criticizing feminism, Islam and immigrants. He has been especially supportive of President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policy, aimed at people in the country illegally.

“Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts,” Yiannopoulos said on X last year.

The British national has most recently worked for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, who performed in New Orleans on Friday evening.

Yiannopoulos rose to fame in the early 2010s as an incendiary writer for the conservative website Breitbart News. He resigned in 2017 after a video of him endorsing pedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologized for the remarks and said he himself was a victim of sexual assault as a minor.

Yiannopoulos’ arrest and deportation come amid a nationwide uptick in detentions as part of Trump’s immigration crackdown.

In social media posts, the Department of Homeland Security touted Yiannopoulos’ arrest and posted a booking photo of him. It added that it encourages people in the country illegally to leave voluntarily, saying the U.S. offers “$3,000 and a free flight to self-deport.”

“We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return,” the department said.

The department did not respond Saturday to questions seeking more details about Yiannopoulos’ legal entry into the U.S. in 2019, including whether he was granted a visa.

Controversy has swirled around the provocateur for years

Far-right conservative activist Laura Loomer swiftly took to social media to applaud Yiannopoulos’ arrest after years of public feuding between the two personalities.

“I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” Loomer said on X.

Controversy around Yiannopoulos ballooned in 2017 when he carried out what he called his “Troll Academy Tour” across college campuses nationwide. Fights broke out when some students protested his appearances and accused him of hate speech, while others celebrated him as a champion of free speech. Around that time Buzzfeed reported on Yiannopoulos’ cozy relationships with self-proclaimed white nationalists.

In recent years Yiannopoulos continued to work in the orbit of conservative activism. In 2022 he was an intern for former U.S. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, according to the Washington Post. He subsequently ran the short-lived 2024 presidential campaign for Ye.

Most recently, Yiannopoulos has worked as a spokesperson for Ye, who has been beset by controversy of his own following antisemitic comments that the rapper has since apologized for.
