text:
British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos was deported to the United Kingdom after his arrest by American immigration authorities, U.S. officials said Saturday.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Yiannopoulos was returned to his home country Friday after being accused of overstaying after entering the U.S. legally in May 2019. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal July 22 after he failed to show up for an immigration hearing, a Homeland Security spokesperson said.

Yiannopoulos was arrested Thursday at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Louisiana and detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement.

Yiannopoulos and his representatives did not respond to requests for comment, and he has not posted on the social platform X since Thursday.

Yiannopoulos backed President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown

Yiannopoulos is a well-known champion of conservative causes and has frequently taken provocative public positions criticizing feminism, Islam and immigrants. He has been especially supportive of President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policy, aimed at people in the country illegally.

“Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts,” Yiannopoulos said on X last year.

The British national has most recently worked for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, who performed in New Orleans on Friday evening.

Yiannopoulos rose to fame in the early 2010s as an incendiary writer for the conservative website Breitbart News. He resigned in 2017 after a video of him endorsing pedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologized for the remarks and said he himself was a victim of sexual assault as a minor.

Yiannopoulos’ arrest and deportation come amid a nationwide uptick in detentions as part of Trump’s immigration crackdown.

In social media posts, the Department of Homeland Security touted Yiannopoulos’ arrest and posted a booking photo of him. It added that it encourages people in the country illegally to leave voluntarily, saying the U.S. offers “$3,000 and a free flight to self-deport.”

“We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return,” the department said.

The department did not respond Saturday to questions seeking more details about Yiannopoulos’ legal entry into the U.S. in 2019, including whether he was granted a visa.

Controversy has swirled around the provocateur for years

Far-right conservative activist Laura Loomer swiftly took to social media to applaud Yiannopoulos’ arrest after years of public feuding between the two personalities.

“I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” Loomer said on X.

Controversy around Yiannopoulos ballooned in 2017 when he carried out what he called his “Troll Academy Tour” across college campuses nationwide. Fights broke out when some students protested his appearances and accused him of hate speech, while others celebrated him as a champion of free speech. Around that time Buzzfeed reported on Yiannopoulos’ cozy relationships with self-proclaimed white nationalists.

In recent years Yiannopoulos continued to work in the orbit of conservative activism. In 2022 he was an intern for former U.S. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, according to the Washington Post. He subsequently ran the short-lived 2024 presidential campaign for Ye.

Most recently, Yiannopoulos has worked as a spokesperson for Ye, who has been beset by controversy of his own following antisemitic comments that the rapper has since apologized for.

text:
A Buffalo-area Republican accused Democratic Erie County Executive Mark Poloncarz of overstepping his authority after the Buffalo Convention Center canceled a two-day Department of Homeland Security career expo set to begin Tuesday because officials objected to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s participation and warned of possible protests.

“The county executive has completely surpassed his power and authority. This was totally inappropriate for him to call on the management of the convention center to cancel this event,” Republican Erie County Legislator Lindsay Lorigo said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Lorigo said she understood discussions about the event were continuing and hoped the center would reverse its decision. She said vendors had invested time and local labor into the expo’s setup.

“I have had discussions with vendors that are already set up there,” Lorigo said. “They’re concerned that they’re going to have to close down their business because they can’t afford the hundreds of thousands of dollars, but now they don’t know who’s going to pay the bill.

“I think he is blowing the safety concern out of the water.”

DHS sharply defended ICE in a statement to Fox News Digital on Friday and rejected criticism as political.

“Our agents are focused on protecting the American people — not entertaining performative outrage. Where is the outrage for Angel families who lost a loved one to illegal alien crime?” a DHS spokesperson said.

“To most Americans, our brave ICE law enforcement are heroes. Eighty percent of Americans support arresting and deporting criminal illegal aliens from American neighborhoods.”

A May Harvard CAPS/Harris online survey found 80% supported deporting immigrants who are in the country illegally and committed crimes.

USAJOBS described the expo as the department’s premier large-scale hiring event. It was open to the public, veterans, military spouses, people with disabilities and recent graduates, with recruiting planned across cybersecurity, intelligence, law enforcement, finance, human resources, immigration services, logistics and transportation security.

New York Labor Department data released Tuesday showed 25,100 people were unemployed in the Buffalo-Cheektowaga area in July. Its 4.4% jobless rate was up from 4.3% a year earlier.

In a joint statement released by Poloncarz’s office Thursday, the county executive said Erie County owns the convention center but does not manage its bookings or daily operations.

Poloncarz said he learned of the expo Wednesday and urged its management corporation to cancel the DHS contract.

“The Buffalo Convention Center is a publicly owned community asset, and I do not believe it should be used to support recruitment efforts that are inconsistent with the values we have repeatedly expressed as a welcoming community,” Poloncarz said.

Convention center President and CEO Patrick Kaler said management first asked DHS to hold the event without ICE.

“When it became clear that was not possible, we made the decision to cancel as we feel it’s in the best interests of our community at this time,” Kaler said.

text:
DAKAR, Senegal (AP) — The United States on Saturday deported dozens of people to the Central African Republic, including an Afghan whose brothers collaborated with the U.S. military, his lawyer and an advocacy group said.

The Afghan man, who is in his early twenties, was granted protection against deportation to Afghanistan by a U.S. judge due to fears of persecution by the Taliban, his lawyer Alma David said.

His family in Afghanistan had received threats from the Taliban because of the work performed by the brothers in support of the U.S. military, according to court documents seen by The Associated Press.

One of the Afghan man’s brothers lives in the United States and served in the Afghan National Army, which collaborated with the U.S military before the Taliban seized power in 2021, David said.

Another one of his brothers was a pilot trained by the U.S. and was killed by the Taliban, she added.

The deportation flight which landed in Central African Republic’s capital Bangui on Saturday, included 12 Afghans and eight Iranians, as well as several people from Nepal and Nicaragua, said Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.

Under a series of often secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to two dozen countries that aren’t their own as it pushes ahead with its immigration crackdown, advocates say. Immigration lawyers say the practice is being used as a legal loophole to indirectly return some asylum seekers to countries they fled. The flight on Saturday is the second to the Central African Republic since June, which carried two dozen migrants, including an Iranian woman facing persecution in her home country.

text:
A federal judge has dealt the Trump administration a significant legal blow, ruling that the administration’s effort to cancel visas and deport noncitizen college students for their pro-Palestinian advocacy and criticism of Israel is unconstitutional.

U.S. District Judge Noel Wise said in her ruling on Friday that the two provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act that the administration cited to initiate deportation proceedings violated the First Amendment.

“Stated plainly, in the United States, freedom of speech belongs to the people. It is not the government’s to take,” she wrote.

Read More on News

The ruling came in a case brought by The Stanford Daily, Stanford University's student newspaper, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, which argued the administration used the provisions to target noncitizen students for deportation based on protected speech, including writing op-eds and attending protests.

It alleged that the administration’s actions had suppressed the speech of noncitizen students who feared that expressing their views could lead to them being targeted for deportation.

Campus Protests

Amid a wider immigration crackdown, the Trump administration started revoking visas and pursuing deportation proceedings against noncitizen students involved in campus protests and political activism last year. The efforts garnered increased attention following the arrests of Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil and Tufts University student Rumeysa Ozturk.

Newsweek has contacted the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, and the White House for comment via emails sent outside regular business hours.

Wise’s ruling echoed a similar decision issued by U.S. District Judge William Young in Boston last year. Young, who was appointed by a Republican president, ruled in a case brought by academic groups that the Trump administration had violated the Constitution when it targeted foreign students for deportation solely for their pro-Palestinian activism and that the policy had chilled political speech.

What The Ruling Said

The lawsuit agreed that Secretary of State Marco Rubio used two provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act to target noncitizens for expressing views. One of the provisions allows Rubio to initiate deportation proceedings against a noncitizen if he personally determines the speech “compromises a compelling foreign policy interest,” while another allows him to revoke the visa of any noncitizen at his discretion.

Attorneys for the student newspaper argued that the provisions violate the U.S. Constitution’s First and Fifth Amendments when applied to constitutionally protected speech.

Wise, an appointee of former Democratic president Joe Biden, agreed.

“When a noncitizen's speech is the but-for factor in a visa revocation and subsequent deportation determination, the government is singling out that speech for disfavored treatment based on its viewpoint or content,” she wrote.

In her ruling, she also wrote that free speech is evidence of a country’s strength.

“Foundational to America’s enduring democracy are our freedoms of speech and the press embodied in the First Amendment,” she wrote.

Free Speech Is Evidence Of Democratic Strength

“In the United States, free speech, including the freedom to criticize the government and its leaders, is not a sign of our democracy’s fragility. It is evidence of its strength. That strength is diminished when members of our society—citizens and noncitizens alike—must self-censor and ‘behave’ or suffer the government’s retaliation.”

She also agreed that the Trump administration’s actions had a chilling effect.

“The government has offered a chilling message regarding protected speech—speak out against Israel or in support of Palestinians and we will revoke your visa and deport you. Behave,” she said. “Noncitizen students heard the warning and heeded. And, as the idiom goes, the silence is deafening.”

She also raised concern that the Trump administration had targeted people for passing on views it wanted to suppress, including those who were critical of Charlie Kirk.

“Tomorrow, or perhaps every today, targets may include anyone in the United States who exercises their freedom of speech to simply express opinions the government does not like,” Wise wrote.

"This downward spiral is antithetical to our Constitution that recognizes our right to speak freely. Here you can simultaneously hate the content of a person’s speech and love the country that cherishes the freedom to allow it."

Plaintiffs Cheer Decision

Conor Fitzpatrick, an attorney with the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, which represented The Stanford Daily, said the judge’s ruling reiterates that free speech is a fundamental right rather than a privilege.

“In America, free speech doesn’t just belong to the people who say things the government agrees with,” Fitzpatrick said in a statement. “Today’s ruling proves that free speech isn’t a privilege, but the inalienable right of every man, woman, and child.”

George Porteous, the editor-in-chief of The Stanford Daily, said: “The reporters in our newsroom shouldn’t have to fear that writing a story will result in their deportation.

“Today’s victory means they won’t have to. The Court’s decision will enable our reporters to focus on what they do best: asking tough questions and reporting the truth.”

text:
By RYAN J. FOLEY Associated Press

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has awarded a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks, saying officers would use them to control detainees and protesters who resist.

ICE moved forward with the purchase despite opposition from civil rights advocates and Democratic members of Congress, who said ICE officers cannot be trusted to use them appropriately.

A notice published in a federal database Thursday said ICE entered into a no-bid contract to purchase the gloves from Compliant Technologies LLC, a Kentucky-based firm that manufactures them. The deal includes acquiring 6,000 of the devices along with support equipment and services over the next six months.

Civil rights advocates have said ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

ICE published the notice hours after a group of U.S. senators, led by Democrat Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada, urged the agency to cancel its plan to buy the gloves. In a letter to ICE’s acting director Thursday, Cortez Masto and 15 of her colleagues in the Democratic caucus questioned ICE’s need for the devices.

“The blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant skepticism about the agency’s professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause,” the letter said.

The senators were the latest to express opposition to the plan, which became public this month when ICE published a notice outlining its intent to purchase thousands of “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” for officers and investigators.

The devices are normal patrol gloves until an officer presses a button to activate the electrical mode. They must be applied directly to someone’s skin to produce a shock that causes pain, which is promoted as a way to gain compliance from people who are resisting. They have been used by some local jails and police departments in recent years.

ICE’s notice said officers would use them in “high-tension environments,” including while making arrests, transporting combative detainees and responding to civil disturbances outside detention facilities.

“It will be used when a subject is actively or passively resisting and an officer needs to gain control quickly to prevent injuries to both parties,” the document said.

It said that the shocks would help “maintain control over inmates and prevent aggression or escape attempts,” allow officers to handcuff people hiding their hands, and assist in crowd control. The goal would be to avoid using “more severe force,” including firearms. The notice said the gloves would be used with “approved policy, training, and accountability standards,” but it did not elaborate.

Cortez Masto and the other senators said in their letter that the device “presents substantial risks if deployed during civil arrests — even more so if it is deployed without clear limits, appropriate training, and comprehensive oversight.” They said ICE must make public details about how officers will be trained and how use of the gloves will be documented and reviewed internally to avoid misuse.

ICE’s parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, reacted defiantly Thursday to critics of the purchase.

“Sanctuary politicians attempting to ban our federal law enforcement from any safety equipment is despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers,” the agency said in a statement.

In a series of posts on X, Loomer blasted Yiannopoulos for his past internship with former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene and his appearances on right-wing commentator Candace Owens’ podcast. Both Greene and Owens are anti-Israel figures who have become critics of Donald Trump and the MAGA movement.

“Milo is going to be deported back to the UK where he can live among the Muslims he has recently chosen to embrace,” Loomer wrote. “Today is a great day for America.” Late Friday, Loomer claimed he was “on an airplane back to the UK.”

Yiannopoulos, a former editor at Breitbart News and onetime beacon of the burgeoning alt-right movement, has a long history of inflammatory comments, and has flirted with Holocaust denial while claiming Jewish ancestry. The Anti-Defamation League labeled him as an “alt right apologist” and a “misogynistic, racist, xenophobic, transphobic troll who is extremely good at getting people to pay attention to him.”

His ascension through the conservative movement was abruptly halted in 2017 after appearing to endorse pedophilia in a video. But the commentator bounced back after developing a relationship with Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West. After Ye began to gain notoriety in 2022 for promoting extreme antisemitic rhetoric, Yiannopoulos joined his long-shot 2024 presidential campaign as chief of staff.

Yiannopoulos also took credit for organizing a dinner in 2022 between Donald Trump, Ye and white nationalist streamer Nick Fuentes, which was widely condemned by both parties. At the time, Yiannopoulos said that he organized it “to send a message to Trump that he has systematically repeatedly neglected, ignored, abused the people who love him the most, the people who put him in office, and that kind of behavior comes back to bite you in the end.”

More recently, when Ye took out a full-page ad in the Wall Street Journal earlier this year to apologize for his antisemitism, Yiannopoulos shared the ad on X — a day after he had posted, “The problem with these kamikaze Jews is they aren’t remotely as likable, human or frightening as Japs.”

Yiannopoulos has said that he is Jewish through his maternal grandmother, though he is a practicing Roman Catholic, and refutes claims of being racist or antisemitic.

In 2019, Yiannopoulos told the Los Angeles Jewish Journal that he is a “paid-up Zionist” who would advocate for a Jewish “super-state” in the Middle East. That interview took place in Berlin, the day after an event where Yiannopoulos spoke to members of the far-right Alternative fur Deutschland party.

Two years earlier, Yiannopoulos had rallied against the City University of New York for hosting Linda Sarsour, a promoter of the Boycott, Divest and Sanctions movement against Israel, as a commencement speaker.

In an April 2026 interview with Owens, who herself has spread antisemitic conspiracy theories, Yiannopoulos compared the Israeli government to Nazi Germany, and said that “Netanyahu’s Israel will have eclipsed Hitler’s Germany by many, many counts, morally speaking, probably by the numbers, too.”

He said that the Netanyahu administration “has gone so far that they’re now willing to sacrifice their own citizens in order to increase their borders.”

text:
Washington is among four states being sued by the Trump administration over in-state college tuition for immigrant students.

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed lawsuits Thursday against Washington, Oregon, Arizona, and New Mexico, arguing their laws illegally give some immigrants tuition benefits that aren’t available to all U.S. citizens, according to a news release from the DOJ. The lawsuits bring the DOJ’s total to 21 states sued over the issue.

“Over 30 years ago, Congress made clear that States cannot put illegal aliens before our Nation’s own citizens,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. stated. “By granting illegal aliens in-state tuition, Washington, Oregon, New Mexico, and Arizona are pushing citizens to the side and ignoring federal law.”

The DOJ is seeking court orders to block the four states from enforcing laws that require colleges and universities to provide in-state tuition rates to all residents regardless of immigration status, as well as state laws providing financial assistance and scholarships to undocumented immigrants.

“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division stated. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”

WA attorney general vows to defend immigrant students

The DOJ is asking courts to block those laws, but the Washington State Attorney General’s (AG) Office is pushing back.

“The administration is challenging longstanding Washington laws that recognize the potential of all our residents regardless of citizenship status,” a spokesperson for the AG’s Office stated. “We look forward to defending Washington law against this politically motivated lawsuit.”

According to the DOJ, the department has won similar lawsuits in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska and Illinois. Those cases resulted in court orders permanently blocking similar state tuition laws. Lawsuits are also pending in 12 other states, including California, New York, New Jersey, Minnesota, Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Maryland and Kansas.

text:
A U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) video showing men in chains being walked onto an apparent deportation flight to Haiti has sparked outrage, with critics accusing Washington of sowing fear in Haitian communities as it ramps up deportations to the violence-hit country.

The video, shared on social media platform X late on Thursday, shows several Black men being led up a set of stairs onto a plane, their hands and feet bound and tied to a chain around their waists.

"Haiti TPS has been TERMINATED," reads the post, which said the footage was from a "Haiti repatriation flight" on Thursday. "Those with terminated TPS are in our nation Illegally. They have two options: LEAVE IMMEDIATELY or be DEPORTED."

TPS refers to temporary protected status, a U.S. designation that allows foreign nationals to live and work in the United States without fear of deportation when conditions in their home countries are deemed too dangerous.

In June, the U.S. Supreme Court allowed President Donald Trump's administration to move ahead with plans to cancel TPS for Haitians despite concerns from lawyers and human rights advocates over deadly gang violence and instability in Haiti.

The move, which impacts more than 300,000 Haitians in the U.S., came into effect in late July.

"The Trump administration terminated TPS for Haitian families and is bragging about sending them back to a war-torn country," the Florida Democratic Party wrote on X, condemning the DHS video. "This isn't strength. It's depravity dressed up as policy."

Democratic Rep. Yassamin Ansari also commented on the post, saying amid "an endless barrage of depravity from the Trump regime ... this is among the worst."

Asked about the criticism, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told CBC News in an email: "The federal courts have ordered the Haitian illegals must leave the U.S. and we have generously made free flights available to the destination of their choice."

Haiti 'remains completely unsafe'

Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the non-profit American Immigration Council, said that "entire communities are living in fear" amid the crackdown on Haitian immigrants.

"Families are being torn apart and others are agonizing about their next steps; basic things [like] how to keep their loved ones safe," Reichlin-Melnick wrote on X, adding that Haiti also "remains completely unsafe."

The Caribbean country experienced a surge in gang violence following the 2021 assassination of then-president Jovenel Moïse, which created a power vacuum and worsened years of insecurity.

According to the United Nations, about 1.5 million Haitians are now internally displaced amid gang-related violence. At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 others were wounded across Haiti between April 1 and June 30 alone.

Last Sunday, at least 47 people, including five children, were killed in a gang attack in Kenscoff, a community overlooking the capital, Port-au-Prince. Dozens of people also were kidnapped.

Indrika Ratwatte, the acting UN assistant secretary general for humanitarian affairs, said on Friday that nearly 200,000 people had been forcibly returned to Haiti in the first eight months of 2026, despite "shocking levels of violence and suffering."

That's a 10 per cent increase compared with the same period last year, Ratwatte said during a special UN Security Council meeting on Haiti. "Many arrive without resources, documentation or support networks, and some have especially urgent protection needs."

Communities brace for more deportations

The New York Times reported this week that the U.S. government plans to speed up deportations to Haiti, going from one flight per month to one per week, after the cancellation of TPS.

CBC News asked the Department of Homeland Security for details on the Haiti deportation flight shown in Thursday's social media video and whether it plans to accelerate further removals.

In an email, a spokesperson said the department does not disclose information about such flights "for operational security and the safety of our personnel."

"Temporary Protected Status is exactly that — temporary. For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent," the spokesperson said.

The New York Times said about 57 deportees arrived in Cap Haitien, a coastal city in northern Haiti, on Thursday's flight. The Miami Herald said children, including a three-year-old born in the U.S., were among those deported. Separately, the DHS said on Monday that it sent 162 Haitians back to the country on an Aug. 20 flight.

U.S. immigration officials arrested controversial British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos on Thursday in New Orleans, according to the Department of Homeland Security.

Immigration officials announced on Friday that Yiannopoulos was arrested at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport and accused him of overstaying after entering the United States legally in May 2019 through New York City. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal on July 22 after Yiannopoulos failed to show up for his immigration hearing, a DHS spokesperson wrote in an email.

“He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a spokesperson for DHS wrote in an emailed statement.

ICE’s online detainee locator did not say where Yiannopoulos was being held, but directed family and legal representatives to the agency’s office in Alexandria, Louisiana, a deportation hub for international flights.

Representatives of Yiannopoulos did not respond to a request for comment. It was unclear whether he has legal representation.

The British national has most recently worked for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, who was scheduled to perform in New Orleans on Friday evening.

Yiannopoulos is a well-known champion of conservative causes and has frequently taken provocative public positions criticizing feminism, Islam and immigrants. He has been especially supportive of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts,” Yiannopoulos wrote on the social platform X last year.

Yiannopoulos rose to fame in the early 2010s as an incendiary writer for the conservative website Breitbart News. He resigned from the company in 2017 after a video of him endorsing pedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologized for the remarks and said he himself was a victim of sexual assault as a minor.

Yiannopoulos’ arrest Thursday comes amid a nationwide uptick in detentions as part of Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Far-right conservative activist Laura Loomer swiftly took to social media to applaud Yiannopoulos’ arrest after years of public feuding between the two personalities.

“I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” Loomer wrote on X.

Controversy around Yiannopoulos ballooned in 2017 when he carried out what he called his “Troll Academy Tour” across college campuses nationwide. Fights broke out when some students protested Yiannopoulos’ appearances and accused him of hate speech, while others celebrated him as a champion of free speech. Around that time, Buzzfeed reported on Yiannopoulos’ cozy relationships with self-proclaimed white nationalists.

In recent years, Yiannopoulos continued to work in the orbit of conservative activism. In 2022, he was an intern for former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, according to the Washington Post. He subsequently ran the short-lived 2024 presidential campaign for Ye. Most recently, Yiannopoulos has worked as a spokesperson for Ye, who has been beset by controversy of his own following antisemitic comments that the rapper has since apologized for.

text:
Democratic California lawmakers are pushing a last-minute bill to ban federal agents from using electric shock gloves, becoming one of the first states in the nation to respond to reports that Immigration and Customs Enforcement plans to purchase thousands of gloves next year as part of the Trump administration’s crackdown.

Democrats this week advanced Assembly Bill 2760, which would prohibit ICE agents and state and local officers from wearing any device that can deliver electric shocks. It would also block California police departments from purchasing the devices with state money.

San Diego Assemblymember LaShae Sharp-Collins, a Democrat, introduced the bill only last week, with days remaining in the legislative session, in a process known as a “gut and amend,” in which an unrelated bill is rewritten and fast–tracked.

ICE Eyes $20 Million Buy of Taser-Like Gloves

The eleventh-hour move follows a notice published earlier this month by the Department of Homeland Security that said ICE is seeking to spend up to $20 million to buy thousands of taser-like gloves from Compliant Technologies, a Kentucky-based company. The product, called G.L.O.V.E. for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, is marketed as a non-lethal, de-escalation device on the company’s website. The Associated Press first reported about the notice.

ICE announced on Thursday it was awarding the Kentucky company a $16.7 million contract for 6,000 pairs of gloves.

“While the gloves are not currently being used in California, waiting for a tragedy to act, in my personal opinion, and so many others, would be something that California could not handle,” Sharp-Collins said at a hearing on Wednesday.

She said the gloves pose a public safety risk and cited the case of a Kentucky man who died after allegedly being shocked 27 times with the gloves and 13 times with a Taser while in jail last year.

Sen. Padilla Wants DHS to Cancel Contract

On Thursday, U.S. Sen Alex Padilla and other congressional Democrats wrote a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin urging the department to cancel its contract with the company providing the gloves, calling them “hand-worn tasers disguised as restraint equipment.”

Civil rights groups strongly support the bill and argue that electric shock gloves are inhumane and an excessive use of force.

“Electroshock gloves by any law enforcement agency makes Californians less safe,” Anallely Martin, of the California Immigrant Policy Center, said at the hearing.

The California State Sheriffs’ Association and numerous other law enforcement groups oppose the bill, arguing it would unnecessarily limit officers’ ability to de-escalate a situation.

“This is a bad policy from a California law enforcement perspective, and it’s really only gonna be a message to the feds that’s going to fail to land,” California State Sheriffs’ Association lobbyist Cory Salzillo said at the hearing.

It’s the latest move by California lawmakers to clamp down on ICE agents in response to President Donald Trump’s sweeping immigration raids. Just this week, Democrats passed a bill that would ban federal agents from working for state or local police agencies and another to make it easier for people to sue agents for civil rights violations.

If Bill Becomes Law, Legal Challenges Expected

In April, a federal court struck down a 2025 law forcing masked immigration agents to identify themselves. Judges ruled the state had stepped out of bounds when it tried to enforce rules against federal officers.

Similar to that law, if Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom signs the new bills, they’re expected to face nearly identical legal challenges.

“States simply can’t regulate how federal officers do their jobs, even if we don’t like how they do their jobs. That’s up to the federal government,” UC Davis law professor Vikram Amar said.

Without a clear argument on how the gloves violate people’s constitutional rights, the legislation would likely hold little weight in court, Amar said.

“It makes a lot of bills like this kind of more performative than real,” Amar said.

text:
Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said Friday that federal officials have not provided his office any information about the fatal shooting last month of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by immigration officers in Houston, so he plans to take the evidence his office has collected so far to a grand jury in the “next few weeks,” in part to compel the release of more details.

Teare said his office also may file a federal lawsuit to force the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, to provide more information.

“We have now kind of put together as much physical evidence as we think we’re going to get and so the next step is to begin to get witnesses into the grand jury so that you get kind of a fuller picture of what eyewitnesses saw,” Teare said.

Although his office now knows the names of the four ICE agents who were pursuing the white van driven by Salgado Araujo early on July 7, Teare declined to identify them, citing grand jury proceedings that are typically secret until suspects have been indicted. Grand juries also have the power to subpoena agencies, including in the federal government, and conduct separate investigations. Teare said the Texas Department of Public Safety, which oversees the Texas Rangers and is conducting its own probe of the shooting, has received some information from DHS that it is sharing with his office to potentially take to the grand jury.

“A lot of our timing is going to be dependent on outside forces, on the cooperation we continue to get from the Texas Rangers, the cooperation we hope to get from DHS’s Office of Inspector General, the cooperation that we’re going to need from other individuals involved and so I really can’t put a true timetable on it,” he said, adding that the grand jury proceedings could ultimately result in a criminal indictment.

Teare, a veteran prosecutor, told the Tribune in the 25-minute interview that crucial aspects of ICE’s pursuit of Salgado’s van and his investigation of the shooting have contrasted sharply with other officer-involved shootings that the district attorney’s office has worked on in the past — even when they involved federal agencies.

The initial tip that set the fatal encounter into motion appeared to be incorrect. ICE agents said they were originally looking for at least one Guatemalan man with a prior deportation order who was also driving a white van in the same heavily Hispanic Houston neighborhood. Salgado and his three passengers — all construction workers on their way to a job that morning — were from Mexico and had no criminal record, their attorneys and families said.

In a new federal filing, ICE officers alleged that DPS provided the initial information about the targeted van.

ICE “had previously received Intel from DPS troopers” of two people in a white van with Texas plates and “sent identification for two subjects,” according to the document, which has since been sealed and is partially redacted. It was filed this week in federal court as part of a petition by attorneys to release one of the passengers from immigration detention.

According to that document, written by ICE officers in their official account of the shooting, neither of the people identified by DPS were the registered owners of the vehicle, so ICE officers conducted their own surveillance.

Weeks prior to the shooting, they had tried to stop the white van, but when its driver fled, officers did not pursue, according to the document. Then, on July 7, ICE officers “observed a white van matching the description” in the same area and pursued it.

A DPS spokesperson, Ericka Miller, wrote in an email that the information ICE agents included in their report was incorrect and that the state police did not provide any information to immigration officers “related to this incident.”

“DPS did not provide any information of any sort to ICE related to the location where the (officer involved shooting) occurred, any vehicles, other individuals or Mr. Lorenzo Salgado Araujo,” she wrote.

Spokespeople for DHS and ICE did not immediately respond to questions about the statements by Teare or DPS. They largely repeated what they’ve said publicly in the past, including that ICE agents were conducting a “targeted enforcement operation” in the area when Salgado Araujo “attempted to evade arrest.”

“From information we are receiving, he rammed an ICE law enforcement vehicle, refused to follow multiple verbal commands, and weaponized his vehicle in an attempt to run over an ICE law enforcement officer resulting in our officer firing his weapon in self-defense,” an unnamed ICE spokesperson wrote in an email.

Those claims have been refuted by the three passengers in Salgado Araujo’s vehicle, two of whom have been released from detention by federal judges who blocked the government from immediately deporting them.

Salgado Araujo’s fatal shooting is among at least three by DHS agents in Texas since Trump returned to office and adds to a growing tally nationwide, including at least two deaths of U.S. citizens in Minnesota. In most of those cases, including all the Texas incidents, DHS agents were not wearing body cameras.

The Minnesota shootings spurred nationwide protests about the harsh tactics of immigration agents there. Yet eight months later, state prosecutors have yet to indict any ICE agents in the shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti and only turned over key evidence to local prosecutors last month, illustrating the difficulty states can encounter when trying to prosecute federal officers.

In Houston, Salgado Araujo’s brother, who was in the front passenger seat and had the most complete view of the shooting, remains in custody. His attorney said this week that the Trump administration has indicated it is likely to finally approve his application for a temporary legal status because he is the witness to a potential crime. His sealed application to be released from custody has “seen movement” this week, attorney Ruby Powers said, but is pending a final decision.

The document released this week also said ICE officers used their emergency lights and sirens when trying to stop Salgado Araujo’s van, although that is not visible in footage of some parts of the pursuit that the Tribune reviewed. None of the ICE officers were wearing body cameras and the agency has maintained that dash cam footage from the two vehicles is not “available.”

Nothing about the ensuing pursuit, fatal shooting, crime scene and investigation has appeared to follow well established procedures, Teare said.

The district attorney’s office, for example, has a long-standing policy that mandates its investigators go to every fatal officer-involved shooting in Harris County. In this case, Teare said his investigators were not given access to the scene until a day later, making its independent investigation much more difficult.

By contrast, he said that the FBI immediately notified his office about the 2018 fatal shooting of a hostage and encouraged it to investigate the death, which eventually resulted in a grand jury declining to indict the federal agent. A federal judge last year found the agent was negligent when he fired the shots, ordering the government to pay about $2 million in damages to Ulises Valladares’ family.

The DA’s office also has not been provided what is called a field operations worksheet, detailing the ICE officers’ justification for stopping Salgado Araujo’s van, as well as ICE’s use of force and pursuit policy.

“This is so unique, having dealt with hundreds of agency officer-involved shootings in my career, to not have this stuff,” Teare said. “I mean, we’re almost through August. This happened July 7, so to not have this is just so out of the norm.”

ICE officers were in unmarked black SUVs and they did not use common emergency lights and sirens as they attempted to stop Salgado Araujo before boxing him in on a narrow residential street partially under construction, Teare said.

Most major state and local law enforcement agencies restrict officers in unmarked vehicles from making traffic stops, according to more than a dozen law enforcement experts who reviewed the available footage. Seth Stoughton, a University of South Carolina professor who focuses on use of force and is a former police officer, said the footage in this case “looks more like a carjacking attempt than it does a police stop.”

Teare echoed those concerns.

“One of the pursuing vehicles couldn’t even make the turn because they were so close,” he said. “It was a pursuit, and you’ve seen the footage. Their emergency equipment was not activated at that time at all.”

Both the chase and the fatal shots, which the vehicle’s passengers said came from an ICE agent on foot who fired through the right window, “wasn’t done the way that any law enforcement agency that I’ve ever worked with would teach their officers to behave,” Teare added.

“The traffic stop was not initiated correctly. The positioning of people is not the way that it’s taught, and so, no, nothing about that was done the way that any law enforcement agency that I’ve worked with would teach their people.”

This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

text:
From Delco to Chesco and Montco to Bucks, what about life in Philly’s suburbs do you want WHYY News to cover? Let us know!

A federal appeals court in Philadelphia ruled Friday that a Trump administration policy mandating detention of nearly all undocumented immigrants violates the Fifth Amendment and federal immigration law.

The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement policy enacted in July 2025 calls for most undocumented immigrants to be detained and held without a bond hearing, even if they have been in the country for years and are pursuing legal status through official channels.

The policy is a drastic shift in decades of government practice, with ICE arguing that a federal immigration statute that mandates detention for people seeking admission to the U.S. at the border also applies to noncitizens who have been living within the country.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit joined seven other federal appeals courts Friday in rejecting that policy, ruling 2-1 that the practice violates the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause as well as federal immigration law. Two other federal appeals courts have ruled in favor of the directive.

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The policy represents a key strategy in the administration’s mass deportation campaign and has played a role in the surge in immigration arrests across the region since President Donald Trump took office again in January 2025.

In response, immigration attorneys have flooded federal courts with habeas corpus petitions, arguing that their clients’ detention is a violation of their constitutional rights. Federal judges across the country have overwhelmingly ruled in their favor.

“Even before the Trump administration began its campaign to detain every person it could round up, immigration detention was a cruel and unnecessary practice,” said Vanessa Stine, senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union of Pennsylvania, in a statement. “But denying bond hearings to the individuals ICE detains is an alarming trend that is blatantly at odds with the plain text of the statute and the Constitution’s guarantee of due process.”

The 3rd Circuit Court’s ruling “represents a milestone in the battle against arbitrary and unlawful detention policies that have been put forth by this administration,” said Mana Aliabadi, an associate attorney at Palladino, Isbell & Casazza, LLC, part of the legal team representing the immigrants who challenged their detention.

The policy has been “part and parcel of the administration’s course to lock people up first and then ask questions later,” she said.

Being detained makes it more difficult for immigrants with pending applications for legal status to work with their attorneys to prepare their cases, as ICE often transfers detainees to other states across the country, Aliabadi said. Their cases are also then sent to detained immigration courts for expedited proceedings.

“Ultimately, the case says that people have a fundamental right to due process and freedom from restrictions on their liberty, whether or not they’re noncitizens in this country,” she said. “So every person deserves an individualized hearing or determination before that liberty or freedom is deprived of them.”

The Justice Department and the ACLU have asked the U.S. Supreme Court to take up the issue in its next term.

Editor’s note: This article has been edited to include comment from Mana Aliabadi, one of the attorneys representing the immigrants who challenged their detention.

name: Human Rights
title: The battle over RAF Barnham: how ominous anti-asylum protests engulfed a small Norfolk town
description:
The first protest against the use of RAF Barnham to house asylum seekers was in June 2026.
“We put it online.” RAF Barnham has been used in many ways over the years.
On my first visit to RAF Barnham, I meet Terry Curtis, 40, one of the protest movement’s organisers.
I talk to a 38-year-old woman who lives near RAF Barnham and is on the protest with her small children.
I leave RAF Barnham with Harry Murray, who has been taking photographs for the Guardian.
text:
‘I don’t talk to mainstream media,” says a young man in an Arsenal shirt. I’ve just asked what brought him to the latest protest against the housing of asylum seekers in Thetford, Norfolk, and his disdain is clear as he goes to warn other protesters of the Guardian’s presence. This isn’t exactly the unity promised by the flyer advertising today’s march: “Everyone welcome: families, friends, dogs. Including the media.”

The protest is planned as a two-mile march from Thetford’s market square to RAF Barnham, a site just over the border in Suffolk, which is due to house asylum seekers while they progress through the system. It is the latest part of a campaign that has lasted the whole summer. Banners line the square, the largest succinctly describing why people are gathering here today: “Thetford and Barnham says no to asylum seekers.”

Some of the protesters are from Thetford, others from farther afield, but mostly Norfolk or Suffolk. I have been visiting Thetford in the weeks before the protest and, while the reasoning of the protesters varies, many say it comes down to numbers. How can this site house 1,250 people when the nearest village has a population of only 600?

Some say the country can’t afford to keep housing asylum seekers as they wait to be processed, or that there are simply too many coming in, or that we don’t know who they are. Asylum seekers are referred to by some here as “boat people” and “invaders”. The suggestion that Britain has lost control of its borders is nothing new. But new theories still materialise. At a protest the week before the march, one attender suggested that people may be being sent intentionally from Iran. “They say that they are sending some of the terrorists over to the UK and we have no idea who comes off the boats,” a protester, David Goulty, told me. “There’s no control on who comes into the country.”

In opposition, Labour criticised the Conservative policy of housing asylum seekers on military bases. But in October last year, now in government, it changed tack. The sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl by a resident of the Bell hotel in Epping, Essex, had prompted months of angry local protests against the housing of asylum seekers in hotels. Keir Starmer announced that military bases would be used once again.

Labour was explicit about the reason for the U-turn: “We know that communities don’t want asylum seekers housed in hotels, and neither does the government, and that’s why we are determined to fix the mess that we’ve inherited by getting a grip of the issue and committing to close every single asylum hotel, saving the taxpayer billions of pounds.”

Typically of Starmer’s time as prime minister, the people he was trying to appease with this policy responded: “Thanks, we hate it.”

Now, the Home Office is actively working to expand or open five sites, two of which are already active. MDP Wethersfield, a former RAF airfield in Essex, houses 800 asylum seekers, but could increase its capacity to more than 1,200. Crowborough training camp in East Sussex plans to increase its numbers from 350 to 540; a volunteer vigilante patrol group has been set up in the area to “protect” locals from migrants. Three large military sites are being readied with a reported capacity of 1,250 each: MOD Bicester in Oxfordshire; RAF Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire; and RAF Barnham.

Much of the classic sitcom Dad’s Army was shot in Thetford, including the external shots of the episode that ends with the show’s most famous joke: “Don’t tell ’em, Pike!” The Guildhall on the market square, where the protesters congregate to start the march today, was often used as a backdrop.

The Dad’s Army museum is on the other side of the Guildhall. One of the protesters is an 80-year-old US air force veteran who thinks the UK should emulate Trump’s immigration policy. He sees a group of tourists being led on the Dad’s Army guided tour and invites them to join the march. It’s clear they would rather hear more tales of Jones, Mainwaring and Pike.

On the other side of the square, Anwar Noor, 63, is selling ice-creams from his truck to people gathering for the march. Noor came to Thetford from Kenya in the 1980s and worked in the Thermos factory for 17 years, before being made redundant when it closed. (Thermos moved manufacturing to Asia in 2000. Other big employers, such as the factory that processed Danepak bacon, have since closed, leading to the loss of hundreds of jobs.) Noor started another business, a scrapyard, before joining the ice-cream trade a couple of years back as he started his semi-retirement.

You could argue that Thetford is East Anglia’s capital of integration. In 1903, it elected the first black mayor in the UK, Allan Glaisyer Minns, who was born in the Bahamas and had trained as a doctor at Guy’s hospital in London. There is an established Portuguese community, congregating this morning at a cafe near the square, drinking bottles of Super Bock beer as a very loud wildlife documentary about porcupines plays on TV. The community moved here in their hundreds in the 2000s, after big East Anglian agribusinesses, including the turkey giant Bernard Matthews, set up recruitment offices in the country.

There is a statue of Duleep Singh, the last maharaja of the Sikh empire, who was exiled to Britain from Punjab and became a favourite of Queen Victoria, living in Elveden Hall, just over the Suffolk border. His son, Prince Freddy Duleep Singh, became a scholar of Norfolk life and gave Thetford the Ancient House, a home thought to have been built in about 1490, which is still used as a public museum.

But, as Ian Jack wrote in 2007, during a visit in which he marvelled at Thetford’s burgeoning Portuguese community, while suggesting the town was already paranoid about immigration statistics: “To compare Prince Freddy with the immigrant ham-slicer or turkey-gutter is of course ridiculous.”

There had already been unrest around immigration when Jack visited the town. In 2004, as New Labour’s second of three terms was nearing its end, Thetford was topping tables for deprivation and child poverty while coming bottom for skills and education. That summer, after England lost to Portugal in the quarter-finals of the European Championship, the Red Lion pub on the market square was besieged by more than 200 hooligans, trapping about 120 people – mostly Portuguese – inside the pub. They pelted the building with bottles and stones, smashed windows and tried to force their way in. Police called in reinforcements from all over Norfolk and several officers and pub customers were said to have sustained cuts from flying glass. It was more than two hours before those inside could leave.

The Red Lion, now a Wetherspoons, feels more sedate today. It sits on the edge of the market square, which, in the sun, feels like a piazza with added pints. And yet Noor, as he doles out ice-creams, says he can understand why people are angry. “You probably noticed as you walked through the town how many shops are closed, post offices gone. All the banks are gone. You can see the centre hollowing out.” Noor says he understands local people’s frustration and that he has never experienced racism in Thetford. But he believes that blaming asylum seekers is “all wrong. We’re all in the same boat.”

At times this August, what has happened in this small Norfolk town has seemed portentous, at risk of provoking another summer of unrest in England, after events in Southport in 2024 and Epping in 2025 led to protests around the country.

At the start of this month, the addresses of some houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) used to house asylum seekers in Thetford were leaked. This led to crowds of vigilantes targeting the properties on 4, 5 and 6 August.

During the second night of unrest, hundreds of people descended on a terrace house on Clover Way in the 70s-built Fairfields estate. Some threw rocks and eggs, smashing an upstairs window, while others attempted to get inside. During these days of disorder, police officers were spat at, while one was hit by a rock and another was bitten. According to police, some of the vigilantes even entered a property and forced out a resident, stealing their mobile phone.

More than 20 people were arrested on suspicion of a variety of offences, including racially aggravated public order, inciting racial hatred and conspiracy to commit aggravated burglary, as well as possession of cocaine with intent to supply, possession of cannabis and driving without insurance.

On the day of the Thetford to Barnham march, I visit Clover Way. The house that was once home to asylum seekers is immediately identifiable by the dried yolk that remains on the windows, almost three weeks after the eggs were thrown.

One of the neighbours comes out to have a cigarette. She tells me she had to flee to a friend’s house over the road on the night the crowds came; since losing her husband last year, she lives on her own. She suggests I speak to her neighbour, John Finch, 91. He says the people who sold the house that was besieged were initially going to sell it to a family, but they were gazumped by a company, which offered more money.

On the night the protesters arrived, the crowds stood on Finch’s flowerbeds and trampled his plants. He saw the melee out of his window, but decided to go to bed. “I slept through it,” he says. He was in the RAF police branch that served in Cyprus when Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots started firing at each other. “I’ve seen worse.”

When the disturbances went viral online, it brought infamy to this quiet street. The next day, film crews arrived, as did people keen to see the newly famous house covered in egg. “There were a lot of people coming,” says Finch. “They were coming in cars and stopping and just looking at it. And I think: it’s an empty bloody house, for Christ’s sake.” He shrugs. “Perhaps it was the highlight of their life.” Thankfully, after those three ugly nights, the violent disorder in Thetford fizzled out. But the anti-asylum protests continued.

The first protest against the use of RAF Barnham to house asylum seekers was in June 2026. Now, every Sunday, they happen like clockwork at 2pm. The week before the march from Thetford town centre to RAF Barnham, I visit the protest camp at the military base.

I park on the dry grass verge and walk towards the protest, noticing a makeshift shed offering drinks to protesters for whatever they can afford. A shirtless fortysomething man with a tan greets me and asks if I want a drink. Clinton Warner grew up across the road from the site and knows its history. He runs a used-car company and each weekend he moves his stock out of the way, so that there is parking space to accommodate the protesters.

Warner tells me a contract worker, tasked with servicing the sewers on the RAF Barnham site, gave him a tipoff about the plan to house asylum seekers there. He decided to blow the whistle. “They were asked to recommission it, so the contractors knew about it seemingly before the councillors,” he says. “We put it online.”

RAF Barnham has been used in many ways over the years. It has been a logistics hub for the RAF, and during the second world war it was a mustard gas and munitions storage facility. After the war, it was commissioned by Churchill to store nuclear bombs and everyone forgot about the mustard gas stored underground. Warner remembers being warned: “Do not remove wildlife from these ponds, do not pick the lilies, do not remove the flowers, leave everything, because it’s all hazardous.”

The use of sites such as Barnham to house asylum seekers isn’t only controversial with concerned residents. Two years ago, the UK parliament’s home affairs select committee wrote that the use of large military sites to house asylum claimants had “generally proved more costly to deliver than hotel accommodation”. Military sites cost more because of the cost of refurbishing them; they are often in a poor state of repair.

When it comes to the asylum issue, the UK government seldom learns the lessons published by parliament. Rather than respond to the evidence, the government seems trapped in a reactionary loop, apparently keen to be seen to do something punitive.

“In policy discourse, there’s this concern about how some asylum accommodation can function as a pull factor,” says Nuni Jorgensen, a researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford. “Politicians often say hotels can work as a pull factor because people imagine that these are fancy hotels and that’s why they come to the UK. But the evidence that we have on that is not very clear.” That hasn’t stopped politicians such as Reform UK’s Nigel Farage making hay with the suggestion. Jorgensen adds, however, that there is a lot of evidence showing that larger sites negatively affect asylum seekers’ wellbeing.

When it comes to housing, asylum planning boils down to three choices. Hotels are cheaper when it comes to housing many migrants at one site. HMOs seem a good option when it comes to integration and infrastructure, but are hampered by the reality of house prices. And then there are military sites, which are notoriously difficult to use for this purpose.

Hotels are easier to source than HMOs, says Jorgensen, but they “have been linked to very poor mental-health outcomes among residents”, as the conditions are often cramped and unclean and isolate them from the community. Dispersal to neighbourhood HMOs has, historically, been the Home Office’s preferred option. “They tend to be cheaper than hotels. They tend to produce the best wellbeing outcomes for asylum seekers. The problem is that they are very hard to find in some areas.”

The failure of the hotels policy and suspicion around private management of HMOs are among the issues that have led to the use of large military sites.

It is clear that these sites are controversial. Along with the volunteer vigilante patrol group in Crowborough, a village near RAF Bicester has voted symbolically to leave the UK over the policy. The use of military sites to house asylum seekers has, in a way, united left and right in opposition, but on very different grounds. Human rights campaigners say they amount to a form of “open-prison camp”, while Reform UK likens them to holiday camps.

On my first visit to RAF Barnham, I meet Terry Curtis, 40, one of the protest movement’s organisers. He was present at the HMO protests in early August, he says, but left “when things escalated … because it’s not what we’re here for”. He says the police were heavy-handed in their tactics; he mentions that a woman on a mobility scooter was pepper-sprayed. No one I speak to who was present at the HMO protests seems to have considered how afraid those living in the affected properties must have been.

Curtis moved to Thetford from south London when he was 15 and still supports Millwall. London accents can be heard all over Thetford. In the 1950s, the town’s population was 5,000. By the end of the 1960s, due to overspill from the capital, it had more than tripled to 17,000. In that booming decade, when new towns were referred to as “pram towns” because of the amount of children being born, Thetford was the fastest-growing in the country.

The Abbey estate was the last to be completed in that period of great expansion. In 1968, it was opened by Labour’s minister for housing, Tony Greenwood, who said the design was “exceptional”. The estate is today the poorest area of Thetford and was one of the locations of the violent protests in early August. Regeneration plans were announced in 2019, which were deeply unpopular with many residents and scrapped by Reform UK when they took over Norfolk county council in May. This was part of a Reform UK surge across the county, except in liberal, urban Norwich.

Curtis says he knows what it’s like to go through hard times: “I’ve been homeless myself … I’ve been in hostels.” The movement isn’t affiliated with any political party, he says, which feels like a stretch. Local Reform UK politicians mingle with the protesters each week, including the councillor Scott Hussey, a former Sun journalist who has moved back to his home town and seems fully committed to the anti-immigration agenda.

It is clear that the rise of Reform, and Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain, in East Anglia has put the wind in the sails of movements such as these. Reform UK now runs the county councils in Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex, in each case unseating the Conservatives, while Restore-backed candidates swept all 10 contested seats they stood for in the May 2026 local elections.

“I feel like we’ve got more inequality than we have equality these days,” says Curtis. “Everybody should be treated the same. And, unfortunately, we’re not. Everything’s going up. Prices are going up. Taxes are going up. But, yeah, people are able to come over here, you know, on boats, seek asylum and then get a home, get a house, get what they want – fed, gas, electric, all paid for by the government, which is inadvertently [sic] the taxpayers. Personally, I think we should close the borders to everybody. Get our own country sorted first.”

A failure of political communication, and the rise of social media that reward extreme content, has led to the anti-asylum narrative in UK politics becoming overwhelming. This isn’t lost on Terry Jermy, the Labour MP who represents South West Norfolk, the constituency that includes Thetford.

Some MPs parachute into a constituency with barely any knowledge of it. Not Jermy. He shot up the ranks of local politics, from town councillor in 2008 to mayor in 2016, before giving Liz Truss her Portillo moment in 2024, when he was unexpectedly elected MP at the expense of the former prime minister.

Jermy’s family has lived in Thetford for hundreds of years. In his maiden speech, in October 2024, he alluded to the fact his dad was one of 13 and his mum had seven brothers. “With nearly 40 aunties and uncles and over 100 cousins, I am sure that I owe at least my first election victory to my grandparents’ love for one another.”

After the HMO attacks, Jermy said the violence was “scaring and terrifying people who live in Thetford, particularly people from minority ethnic communities who are contacting me terrified that they are going to be misidentified as an asylum seeker and attacked”.

Jermy says he can see why the hotels policy had to change – “it’s not a good use of taxpayers’ money” – and isn’t against the use of military bases in principle. But he strongly opposes the use of Barnham. “I get branded a hypocrite when I say that Barnham’s not appropriate,” he says. “But if you’ve been to Barnham [the village rather than the military base], you will see that it’s relatively small. It’s in the middle of nowhere and it’s going to cost the government a fortune to put in the sewage and electricity and everything else that’s needed to make it work. I suspect, once they’ve done their calculations, they will realise that the cost-benefit rules it out.”

He points out that Barnham was only ever an overflow base for Honnington, a much bigger base nearby. Barnham has been empty for a long time and Jermy says a lot of the buildings are in a state of disrepair, “so new modular units will have to be built” to accommodate people.

The truth is, like a lot of asylum policy, this plan doesn’t feel very well thought-out. Meanwhile, the language used by the Home Office has been sloppy to the point of stoking rage, he says. “In the official government factsheet about Barnham, they referred to the people due to be based there as ‘illegal migrants’. They are asylum seekers. They are waiting to be processed.”

Jermy has flagged this with Home Office ministers, but he is facing an uphill battle with his constituents over a subject that is confusing at the best of times. “Most people don’t understand the difference between refugee, asylum seeker and economic migrant. And we’ve got a lot of work to do in this country to educate people about that, but also to talk more positively about immigration and its contribution to society.”

He doesn’t blame local residents for being angry. “These people have been failed,” he says. “They’ve been failed by decades in which people don’t shop in town centres any more and manufacturing is on the decline. And the vast majority of jobs locally are minimum wage. Our schools are rubbish and our healthcare system is rubbish. They’re going to be grumpy and they’re looking for somebody to blame. And rather than us, as a Labour government, articulating, actually, that it’s greed and austerity that are driving this, a lot of the language that we have used, trying to out-Reform Reform, has aided and abetted a lot of those concerns.”

At 1.30pm on Sunday, the march from Thetford to Barnham is due to begin. A group of women assemble behind the main banner. The march starts and passes through town. Shoppers stop and stare at the collection of union and St George’s flags.

The protesters move past a golden statue of Thomas Paine, the Thetford-born autodidact, founding father of the US and author of Rights of Man. The statue glints in the sunshine as Louis Armstrong’s What a Wonderful World drifts out of a speaker on wheels, being pulled by a female protester. The next track is Vera Lynn’s The White Cliffs of Dover. As we turn a corner, a horse-drawn hearse, crewed by three funeral directors in traditional garb, arrives out of nowhere, carrying a cardboard coffin with “DEMOCRACY” written on its side.

A handful of people watch the protesters pass. One or two are clapping. I don’t come across anyone who is vocally against the protests, despite talking to scores of people. It occurs to me later that I didn’t meet anyone who wanted to say anything in support of asylum at all.

And yet, the turnout of 130 people or so tells its own story. Although the march was billed as a community event, it hasn’t attracted a big crowd. One of the main chants as we walk out of town is distinctly un-family-friendly: “Deport, deport, deport the fucking lot.”

Jermy isn’t here because, although he agrees that Barnham should not be used to house asylum seekers, the protests have attracted gestures of support from not only Reform UK and Restore, but also the far-right party Britain First. During the protests at RAF Barnham, says Jermy, “there have been speeches on the stage which have basically been outright racist and disgusting and my presence would be seen as condoning that behaviour”.

We are on the straight road out to Barnham when the crowd starts cheering for a young man who is standing on the side of the common, setting off a flare attached to a St George’s flag. Acrid smoke spreads across the march. As two police officers approach the young man, an accomplice on a motorbike arrives, speeding him off towards a housing estate, to more cheers.

The march crosses the border from Norfolk to Suffolk, exiting Jermy’s constituency and entering the Bury St Edmunds and Stowmarket constituency of his fellow Labour MP Peter Prinsley. “It’s affecting the whole country,” says Jean Glasdale, 73, who has come to the march from just outside Bury St Edmunds. What does she want the government to do? “I want them to deport them,” she says. “I want to be able to walk safely. I mean, they’re not just raping children, they’re raping pensioners like me. I want to feel safe in my own country.”

Talk of rape, amplified and distorted, fills the air at events like this. After we reach Barnham, male speaker after male speaker from Reform UK and smaller fringe parties follow each other on to the small stage with ever greater claims about what rape statistics suggest about migrant behaviour, generating fear about the threat posed by “undocumented, fighting-age men”.

What is clear from the statistics is that most rapes are perpetrated by men already known to the victim. But the image of men marauding the countryside and making women unsafe is potent and heavily exploited. I talk to a 38-year-old woman who lives near RAF Barnham and is on the protest with her small children. She is full of fear, she says, about what she sees as the threat posed by asylum seekers. She is so scared, in fact, that she thinks they should be held in detention offshore: “The safety of people is paramount. If they’re off from the main island – you know, if they’re off, say, Shetland or wherever – it’s another barrier and it’s another bit of protection for us.”

Safety concerns trump talk of specific ideologies – and sometimes reality. “No, there’s no far right,” says Curtis, the organiser. “It doesn’t matter whether you’re left or right wing. This is not what it’s about. It’s just about the community – all the communities getting together to feel safe. You know, everybody’s concerned for the safety of the whole area. Because the people that are going to be put here are going to be able to do whatever they want, whenever they want.”

It’s a message that magnifies the threat of foreign-born men. “It’s been going on since for ever,” says Vron Ware, author of Return of a Native, of the exploitation of these primal fears of rape by “others” and “invaders”. Ware’s book is a reckoning with rural England and chancers such as Lowe and Farage who try to exploit its insecurities.

In the 1980s, Ware was the editor of the anti-fascist publication Searchlight. “I’ve got a poster of an old fascist march in the 70s where someone’s got a placard that says: ‘75% of rapings are done by immigrants.’ It’s just a trope that never goes away.”

After the march, I ask Curtis how he thought it went. He seems a little disappointed with the turnout. He says he is going to take some time out from organising, which has taken its toll.

I leave RAF Barnham with Harry Murray, who has been taking photographs for the Guardian. We trudge along the side of the road, articulated lorries rushing past, until we reach a footpath through a field. As we make our way towards town, passing a few cows, I think about how angry everyone is – not just at events like today, but everywhere and all the time – and how draining it feels.

text:
British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos was deported to the United Kingdom after his arrest by American immigration authorities, U.S. officials said Saturday.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Yiannopoulos was returned to his home country Friday after being accused of overstaying after entering the U.S. legally in May 2019. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal July 22 after he failed to show up for an immigration hearing, a Homeland Security spokesperson said.

Yiannopoulos was arrested Thursday at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Louisiana and detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement.

Yiannopoulos and his representatives did not respond to requests for comment, and he has not posted on the social platform X since Thursday.

Yiannopoulos backed President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown

Yiannopoulos is a well-known champion of conservative causes and has frequently taken provocative public positions criticizing feminism, Islam and immigrants. He has been especially supportive of President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policy, aimed at people in the country illegally.

“Zero immigration for the next 20 years. No ifs, no buts,” Yiannopoulos said on X last year.

The British national has most recently worked for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, who performed in New Orleans on Friday evening.

Yiannopoulos rose to fame in the early 2010s as an incendiary writer for the conservative website Breitbart News. He resigned in 2017 after a video of him endorsing pedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologized for the remarks and said he himself was a victim of sexual assault as a minor.

Yiannopoulos’ arrest and deportation come amid a nationwide uptick in detentions as part of Trump’s immigration crackdown.

In social media posts, the Department of Homeland Security touted Yiannopoulos’ arrest and posted a booking photo of him. It added that it encourages people in the country illegally to leave voluntarily, saying the U.S. offers “$3,000 and a free flight to self-deport.”

“We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return,” the department said.

The department did not respond Saturday to questions seeking more details about Yiannopoulos’ legal entry into the U.S. in 2019, including whether he was granted a visa.

Controversy has swirled around the provocateur for years

Far-right conservative activist Laura Loomer swiftly took to social media to applaud Yiannopoulos’ arrest after years of public feuding between the two personalities.

“I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” Loomer said on X.

Controversy around Yiannopoulos ballooned in 2017 when he carried out what he called his “Troll Academy Tour” across college campuses nationwide. Fights broke out when some students protested his appearances and accused him of hate speech, while others celebrated him as a champion of free speech. Around that time Buzzfeed reported on Yiannopoulos’ cozy relationships with self-proclaimed white nationalists.

In recent years Yiannopoulos continued to work in the orbit of conservative activism. In 2022 he was an intern for former U.S. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, according to the Washington Post. He subsequently ran the short-lived 2024 presidential campaign for Ye.

Most recently, Yiannopoulos has worked as a spokesperson for Ye, who has been beset by controversy of his own following antisemitic comments that the rapper has since apologized for.

text:
A United States federal judge has ruled that President Donald Trump’s administration violated the constitutional rights of international students when it sought to punish them for criticising Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

In California on Friday, District Judge Noel Wise heaped criticism on the US Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) after the agencies attempted to deport noncitizens over protected speech.
