text:
Immigration arrests across Washington state shot up to a new high over the summer, reflecting a nationwide surge in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The newly published records show which cities in Washington state were the hardest hit.

Roughly 700 people were arrested each month in June and July. Just to compare, in just those two months of this year, ICE arrests eclipsed all the recorded arrests during the first seven months of 2025. About 24 people were detained in June and July 2024 during the final year of former President Joe Biden’s term.

Washington hasn’t seen a day without an ICE arrest since late March, according to ICE records. In Seattle, fewer and fewer days also go by without an arrest, often only pausing on the weekend, according to records released this week from the Deportation Data Project based at the University of California and analyzed by KUOW.

The project obtains records of ICE arrests and detentions through Freedom of Information Act requests to the Department of Homeland Security. For the first time, the records published by researchers also now breakdown arrests by city.

From January through the end of July, here are the top cities where people have been arrested.

Yakima: 522 arrests

Seattle: 477 arrests

Tukwila: 362 arrests

Spokane: 342 arrests

After that, cities like in Tacoma, SeaTac, and Kent each have had more than 100 people arrested over the past several months.

Nearly all the arrests take place in the community through traffic stops, at check-ins or other enforcement. The ICE records refer to these as “at large” or street arrests.

A small percentage of arrests, categorized as “custodial arrests” happen through transfers from state or federal prisons to ICE custody. These transfers are a level of state cooperation with immigration enforcement that’s allowed under the Keep Washington Working Act.

According to the data, the majority of street arrests are people who have no criminal record.

Unlike previous and highly visible ICE operations in other states, much of enforcement in Washington is often discreetly happening early in the morning or in the evening hours.

“It felt like we were chasing ghosts,” said David Morales. He leads the immigrant response teams for the Yakima Immigrant Response Network, which has been operating since President Donald Trump’s first term.

Before this summer's surge of ICE arrests and detentions in Seattle, cities like Yakima had already been feeling the significant effects of ramped up immigration enforcement and arrests. Initially it was a challenge for the network’s efforts to document and report ICE arrests to the public.

“It was like trying to find evidence of what had occurred because these things would happen, and all we would have is a smashed car window or a vacant car,” Morales said.

Since then the Yakima network has made strides, including having local content creators help vet reports online, and tracking reports posted to social media.

“Over the course of the last year and a half, we've gotten a bit more community trust, and community members know to record these things. We're able to find recordings of ICE arrests much more commonly than we used to find,” Morales said.

Many of the people arrested in Washington state are taken into custody during a vehicle stop. Along with targeted enforcement, immigration enforcement will use racial profiling, and other factors, to identify someone to arrest while out on patrol. They access driver and license plate records managed by the Washington Department of Licensing and Washington State Patrol, putting those state agencies at odds with state laws that were passed in effort to limit the amount of cooperation between Washington state and federal immigration enforcement agencies.

“There are many victories that turn out to not be victories and not to have any real effect,” Morales said.

The governor's office said there is no immediate way to address this incongruence in the near term. They want to avoid fully shutting off all access to the federal government in order to keep information flowing for public safety concerns — such as law enforcement that targets human trafficking.

Morales also said many arrests are also frequently happening outside of local courts, and points to the Courts Open to All Act, passed the year after the Keep Washington Working Act, as also floundering. That act sought to prevent immigration enforcement from interfering with local court matters.

“It's the same thing with the face mask law [that] has been blatantly violated every single day,” he said. “I think the passage of the law encouraged them to put on the mask as a political signal of rebellion against the state.”

Since last September Morales said the Yakima network has launched a humanitarian department helping families who’ve lost a breadwinner with legal aid, meal boxes, gas cards, and other basic supplies. In some cases they’ve also been helping families secure U.S. and Mexican passports to leave the country if the family chooses to deport together.

“We're… getting basically move-out packages with suitcases and, and, and other similar items,” Morales said. “It's been very difficult for the volunteers, but it's also been very rewarding for the volunteers.”

Enforcement has struck at the sense of safety of many mixed immigration status communities. Morales points to a decrease in community vitality and a reported decline in Latino businesses, the hardest hit community by immigration enforcement in Yakima.

Other cities and communities are also feeling the effects, as Renton Councilmember Carmen Rivera documented in a social media post this week after an encounter with ICE agents.

“if you are an elected official, it is the least that you can do to confront ICE in your neighborhood,” she said. “We have the position, the privilege, and the platform. Eyes are on us, and it is up to us to protect our neighbors.”

Rivera joined a group of her neighbors in a standoff with ICE agents Thursday that lasted 45 minutes, she said. Officers were parked in front of her neighbor’s home in two SUVs with tinted windows, one identified with ICE logo on the side of the vehicle. Inside she said she saw agents with face coverings.

She approached one of the ICE officers asking why they were in her neighborhood. She was told they had a warrant for one of their neighbors who was inside their home.

“ He would not show me this warrant and basically said they would not leave until they were able to serve this warrant, which they were not able to show me,” she posted online.

After 45 minutes, Rivera said the ICE agents left. She said it was a case of mistaken identity. Her neighbor was a U.S. citizen.

But the neighborhood is now vigilant, expecting ICE agents to return. The daughter of a police officer, Rivera said Trump’s immigration enforcement crackdown is not making her community safer.

“ These cowards aren't going to stop. It's gonna be up to us to keep us safe,” she said. “So stay vigilant, stay safe, join a rapid response group if you can, get to know your neighbors, take care of each other, and please be safe.”

text:
The Assembly passed a bill Friday to impose an annual tax on private detention centers, sending the legislation to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk.

Assembly Bill 1633 establishes the Private Detention Facility Tax Law, which would impose an annual 25% tax on operators of private detention centers. The money collected from the tax would be deposited into a “Due Process for All Fund” in the State Treasury, which would finance immigration-related services and support for communities impacted by detention centers.

The legislation passed by a 30-10 vote in the Senate Thursday and a 54-17 vote in the Assembly, both along party lines.

Assemblymember Matt Haney, D-San Francisco, said he authored the bill in reaction to reports of inadequate living conditions in California’s private immigration detention facilities. Allegations of insufficient medical care and lack of hygiene products, edible food and clean drinking water were among these concerns, according to Haney.

“For years, (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) has fueled a system that profits from human suffering and family separation, outsourcing detention to private corporations who rake in profits while people endure dangerous, inhumane conditions,” Haney said in a statement to The Sacramento Bee. “Corporations running these facilities are being paid hundreds of millions to detain people in cruelty right here in California, and it has to end.”

The legislation comes shortly after two private detention facilities opened in California, bringing the state’s total to eight. The California City Immigration Processing Center, which opened in August 2025, is California’s largest immigrant detention facility with 2,560 beds. This April, for-profit prison company Geo Group opened the 700-bed Central Valley Annex facility in McFarland, Calif.

The construction of new detention centers in California is part of President Donald Trump’s nationwide effort to expand ICE arrests and detentions. The Trump administration announced a $45 billion expansion of detention facilities nationwide in February.

“What we’re seeing across the country shows the real-world consequences of ICE’s unchecked power, putting communities and lives at risk for profit with zero accountability,” Haney said.

Opponents to the legislation have said imposing a tax on detention facilities would impede the activities of federal law enforcement officials. Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, voiced his dissent in a May 27 Assembly floor hearing, saying the measure would lead to the closure of immigration detention facilities.

“It unfairly smears and defames the good men and women of federal law enforcement who are just doing their jobs,” DeMaio said. “Not only are you not helping get the criminals out of these communities, you’re gonna release them back into the communities for them to re-commit crimes.”

However, the bill’s supporters maintain the tax would only apply to private civil detention facilities, which do not hold individuals charged with crimes. While the bill would likely impose a fiscal burden on detention facilities, it does not mandate their closure.

“People continue to be detained…with no meaningful end in sight,” said Assemblymember Juan Carrillo, D-Palmdale, during the hearing. “AB 1633 says that if corporations are going to operate detention facilities in California and generate massive revenues from them, they should help pay for the harm and public cost created in our communities.”

The bill has the support of over 100 organizations, including legal aid groups, immigrant rights advocates and community alliances. The bill is co-sponsored by the California Immigrant Policy Center and Services Immigrant Rights Education Network, who advocate for the human rights of detained individuals.

“People have shared stories about their loved ones being denied medical care…and not being able to receive healthy food or adequate water inside the detention centers,” said Shiu-Ming Cheer, deputy director of immigrant and racial justice at the California Immigrant Policy Center. “These facilities are being operated with little to no accountability…it’s really unacceptable. California can and hopefully will do more through this bill to ensure that we protect the rights of Californians.”

text:
An influential Haitian businessman, who spent 332 days in immigration detention in South Florida after Secretary of State Marco Rubio determined that his presence could have serious adverse consequences on U.S. foreign policy, has reached an agreement with the Trump administration that ended his detention.

Dimitri Vorbe, whose high-profile immigration case became a test of the U.S. government’s authority to detain immigrants under a little-used foreign policy provision of immigration law, was released from the Krome Detention Center on Tuesday.

But his freedom comes with a condition: He has agreed to leave the United States, ending further litigation over his detention.

Under an agreement field in federal court in Miami, Vorbe waived a decision on a bond hearing that a federal judge had ordered in his case challenging his detention, and instead agreed to an order of removal. He must leave the U.S. by Sept. 1 for an unspecified third country that has agreed to admit him. Both parties agreed to keep the country out of the public record following a previous deal that was nixed after it was leaked.

The agreement marks an end to a prolong legal battle in which the Department of Homeland Security sought to keep the married father of three in mandatory detention without a bond hearing, arguing his case was not reviewable because of Rubio’s foreign policy determination.

It also comes after the Trump administration failed to present evidence at Vorbe’s bond hearing substantiating its most serious claim following his Sept. 23, 2025, arrest outside his Miami home by Immigration and Customs Enforcement: that “he engaged in a campaign of violence and gang- upport that contributed to Haiti’s destabilization.”

During the bond hearing before an immigration Judge Romy Lerner, Justice Department attorney Vincent Calarco presented no evidence establishing those allegations as he argued Vorbe represented a potential foreign policy danger as stated in a letter from Rubio.

Instead, the government’s filing included a Haitian Times story of Vorbe’s arrest, blog and social media posts, a picture of his home on Zillow, old traffic offenses and a vague article by another unknown online publication insinuating allegations about him. They also included information about the earnings of a company, Société Générale Group, a European banking group with no apparent connection to Vorbe or his family.

The government also included a post about Vorbe’s winnings at a 2021 poker tournament at Seminole Hard Rock.

Counter arguments

“National security considerations should be part of a reasonable basis to deny release on bond,” Calarco argued to the judge stressing Rubio’s letter and arguing that Vorbe lied about his criminal history when he applied for Temporary Protected Status.

“If this court was to issue a bond, the concern is that the respondent would be a flight risk,” Calarco added. “He has the resources to not come back to the next court hearing.”

Vorbe’s lawyers countered with documents intended to show that he was neither a danger nor a flight risk. They included evidence that he had received visas from several countries, letters from U.S. citizens attesting to his character and an order from the Court of First Instance in Port-au-Prince withdrawing an indictment against him declaring any related warrant null and void.

“He’s long come and gone from the United States without incident, attending school here as a child, later graduating from FIU with a degree in accounting,” Patrick Taurel, one of Vorbe’s attorneys said during the bond hearing.

He noted that Vorbe, 53, had legally entered the U.S. on Jan. 4, 2020, on a visa, and prior to its expiration had filed to extend his stay and had also applied for adjustment of status and TPS.

Taurel said a letter the Haitian government sent to ICE, asserting Vorbe had been criminally charged in Haiti and requesting his return, was “a sham.”

He noted that the Haitian government did not seek Vorbe’s extradition through the Justice Department.

“Why do this? Probably because the criminal charges referenced in that letter were an absolute sham, filed pursuant to a complaint that was brought by lawyers who were not even authorized to represent the Haitian government as prosecutors,” Taurel said.

Political feud

The case dated back to the administration of Haiti President Jovenel Moïse, when Vorbe and the late president were engaged in a bitter political and economic feud. Moïse publicly accused Vorbe and members of the country’s economic elite of being responsible for Haiti’s problems. Moïse moved against Vorbe’s electricity-generating company and its assets.

“The record before the immigration court in Mr. Vorbe’s case revealed that the U.S. government had nothing to justify locking him up for 11 months,” Taurel told the Miami Herald.

Taurel said the case demonstrates what he described as the sweeping nature of the foreign policy provision used against his client, as well as others by the Trump administration.

“When the government seeks to remove you from the United States under the so-called foreign policy ground of deportability, you do not get anything resembling due process,” he said. “What you get is an affront to even the most basic notions of fairness.”

Taurel accused Rubio and the administration of relying on “threadbare allegations” as evidence to detain and deport law-abiding permanent residents and visa holders, no matter how false or unsubstantiated those allegations may be.

“Congress must rein in this power, which was declared unconstitutional on three independent grounds by the only court to have reached the merits of its legality, and which this administration has weaponized to go after political dissidents to appease foreign governments and suppress protected speech,” he said.

Rubio has applied the same “foreign policy ground” letter to a number of other individuals, including one-time Haitian presidential hopeful Pierre Réginald Boulos, who also departed the U.S. earlier this year in a deal with the administration.

Vorbe’s release came after a significant victory in his federal court challenge to his prolonged detention. The deal between him and the government means he will give up his right to a ruling on his request to be released on bond. Under the deal, Vorbe has already provided the Department of Homeland Security with his itinerary to leave the U.S.

Massive backlog

U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles ruled on Vorbe’s case after a Miami Herald article detailing how the judge, 53 days after hearing Vorbe’s habeas petition, still had not issued a ruling and how his case was part of a record number of immigration-related habeas corpus cases in South Florida courts, creating a massive backlog. Habeas corpus cases are challenges in federal court of detention or imprisonment.

In his ruling Gayles rejected the government’s argument that Vorbe could be held in mandatory detention without a bond hearing simply because of Rubio’s determination in a letter. Though he stopped short of ordering Vorbe’s immediate release or overturning Rubio’s decision, Gayles ordered immigration authorities to provide Vorbe with a bond hearing by Aug. 24, or release him under reasonable conditions of supervision.

Vorbe’s lawyers had asked Gayles to hold the bond hearing himself. He declined, and instead the hearing took place before an immigration judge at Krome. Under the agreement DHS is barred from seeking another country other than the one both sides agreed to.

Ira Kurzban, one of the country’s preeminent immigration attorneys, said the settlement came at a cost to American taxpayers and sharply criticized the Trump administration’s handling of the case.

“The losers in this agreement are the people of the United States,” he said.

Kurzban, whose Miami firm is among a group of firms suing the Trump administration over the termination of legal protections for more than 300,000 Haitians, criticized the administration over its treatment of people “who have no criminal record, who had lawful status in the U.S.” and had been contributors until their status was taken away. DHS had cited Vorbe’s detention as evidence on why TPS should end, an argument a district judge in Washington rejected when she issued a hold on the termination before being overturned by the Supreme Court.

“The cost to keep Mr. Vorbe in detention for a year for no reason has cost American taxpayers hundreds of thousands of dollars,” Kurzban said. “The legal work defending such unlawful actions, including Rubio’s phony claims that it is in the ‘national interest’ to do so, without providing evidence or a meaningful trial, is a blight on the Constitution and a national disgrace.”

text:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- A newly released watchdog report from the Department of Homeland Security found that as Immigration and Customs Enforcement shifted priorities toward civil immigration enforcement, federal efforts targeting fentanyl trafficking declined significantly.

According to the federal investigators, Homeland Security Investigations' level of effort on fentanyl investigations decreased between fiscal years 2024 and 2025 as resources were redirected to immigration enforcement.

The report found fentanyl investigations fell by 24%, while investigative hours devoted to countering fentanyl declined by 30%. Fentanyl seizures also dropped by 39%.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

The findings come after fentanyl was designated a weapon of mass destruction by President Donald Trump last year.

"The statistics are quite frankly shocking," former Homeland Security Acting Undersecretary for Intelligence and ABC News contributor John Cohen told the I-Team.

Cohen said the shift in priorities reflects the consequences of allocating finite federal law enforcement resources to different missions.

"What we are seeing is that Homeland Security investigations have diverted personnel away from conducting human trafficking investigations, narcotics investigations, gang investigations, so they can increase the amount of hours that they work on civil immigration enforcement," Cohen said.

SEE ALSO | Chicago immigration judge orders removal of 6 kids as green card applications remain pending

The inspector general report highlighted a key finding that competing mission priorities led to a significant decrease in HSI investigative hours. The report included a chart showing immigration investigations increased sharply over the past two fiscal years while fentanyl investigations declined.

The decrease in investigative activity corresponded with a nearly 40% reduction in HSI fentanyl seizures, according to the report.

Cohen said the trend raises concerns at a time when law enforcement agencies are confronting evolving threats.

"This is not the time to be taking resources away from drug gang enforcement from terrorism investigations because we're dealing with terrorists and traffickers that are only becoming more sophisticated and better able to to transit drugs and other potential harmful substances into the United States," he said.

SEE ALSO | DEA warning of heightened threat as synthetic drugs creep at alarming rates into Chicago

The impact of competing priorities is not limited to Homeland Security Investigations. As previously reported by the I-Team, Joint Terrorism Task Force assets in Chicago were used to support immigration arrests. FBI Chicago told the I-Team last year that the work had not affected its goal of preventing terrorism.

Cohen said other federal agencies also have been affected.

"DEA, FBI, Marshal Service, alcohol, tobacco, firearms, even the United States Coast Guard are taking critical law enforcement resources away from interdicting drugs, investigating gangs, preventing violent crime, so they can engage in civil immigration enforcement," he said.

The decline in fentanyl seizures by Customs and Border Protection was even greater over the same period, according to the report. CBP fentanyl seizures fell 45% from fiscal year 2024 to fiscal year 2025.

ICE agreed with all recommendations in the inspector general's report, including reviewing staffing levels and redirecting agents to fentanyl investigations as needed.

title: Cooper, Whatley on immigration: A fight over how to focus enforcement - WRAL
authors: Will Doran, WRAL state government, Will Doran, WRAL state government
description:
And as those deportation efforts ramp up nationwide, immigration policy is in the spotlight in North Carolina’s race for an open seat in the U.S. Senate.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Roy Cooper hasn’t gone as far as other Democrats around the country in calling for the abolition of Immigrations and Customs Enforcement.
Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who is endorsed by Trump, wants to keep forging ahead with the president’s more aggressive immigration crackdown.
Whatley has suggested Cooper is too aligned with national Democrats on issues of drugs and the border.

text:
Federal immigration officials arrested 50,000 people on immigration charges in July, the highest total so far of President Donald Trump’s second term in office. And as those deportation efforts ramp up nationwide, immigration policy is in the spotlight in North Carolina’s race for an open seat in the U.S. Senate.

About 1 million immigrants are estimated to live in North Carolina, including 440,000 naturalized U.S. citizens, according to federal Census data. Data is less clear on the other several hundred thousand non-citizen immigrants, but some estimates predict that they’re split about half-and-half between those who are here legally or not.

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Roy Cooper hasn’t gone as far as other Democrats around the country in calling for the abolition of Immigrations and Customs Enforcement. But he has said immigration agents need to face more accountability. Since Trump retook office last year, dozens of people have died either in shootings by immigration agents, or while in custody at immigrant detention centers. Some of the dead were Americans.

“They are killing and detaining American citizens, including people with no criminal records and it must stop,” Cooper wrote in a recent social media post.

Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who is endorsed by Trump, wants to keep forging ahead with the president’s more aggressive immigration crackdown.

He and his campaign — in speeches, official policy platforms and responses to WRAL’s questions — have said that if elected to the Senate, he’d vote for whatever Trump wants on immigration, as well as whatever is needed after Trump is no longer in office to continue his same approach.

“President Trump ran on securing our borders … and it's tremendously important for us to reflect on that and look at where we are today versus where we are during Joe Biden's tenure,” Whatley said Friday.

At a roundtable event put on by his campaign, Whatley was flanked by women who had lost family members to crimes committed by immigrants — or to opioid overdoses, which Whatley blamed on immigrants.

Whatley isn’t the first Republican politician to blame immigrants for the opioid epidemic, although the data doesn’t necessarily back it up. Most illicit fentanyl is made in Mexico, but it’s typically smuggled into the U.S. by American citizens, according to government data and policy analysts. And they typically bring it in through legal ports of entry, not by sneaking over the border. About 86% of the people convicted of trafficking fentanyl between 2019 and 2023 were U.S. citizens, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission.

Whatley has suggested Cooper is too aligned with national Democrats on issues of drugs and the border. Cooper has pointed to his record as attorney general to show that he’s tough on drug trafficking and willing to deport violent criminals.

After Cooper became governor, Trump appointed him to help lead a task force on fighting the opioid epidemic. Among the other task force leaders was Pam Bondi, who Trump would later put in the charge of the U.S. Department of Justice.

Whatley also suggested there needs to be more money spent on immigration enforcement, while speaking Friday with Paul Perez, the president of a national union of Border Patrol agents that has endorsed Whatley. “I am going to support you,” Whatley told Perez. “I'm going to fight for you. And I'm going to make sure that we have the laws in place. And you have the funding in place.”

Trump pledged to deport millions of immigrants as part of his 2024 presidential campaign. But so far — and despite an extra $170 billion Republicans in Congress gave him last year to hire more immigration agents and implement other border security measures — his Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents have made 610,000 arrests, according to reporting this month by the Marshall Project.

It’s unclear how many of those have been deported; there have been frequent reports of legal immigrants and U.S. citizens being wrongfully arrested in immigration raids — including a Raleigh native who is fighting the government for damages over his detention last year in an ICE raid, which he blames on racial profiling.

Many of the people who have been arrested by ICE have no criminal record, and critics of Trump’s push have said it focuses too heavily on targeting people who have lived peacefully and constructively in the U.S. for years, working despite their lack of legal status. Some critics have questioned Trump’s strategy, including raids on job sites, suggesting his administration should take a more targeted approach to root out criminals.

Cooper recently wrote on social media: “Border Patrol and ICE should do their jobs to make sure our borders are secure and violent criminals here illegally are deported.”

Whatley, however, said Cooper as governor spent years fighting against ICE being able to do just that.

Three times during his eight years as governor, Cooper vetoed bills passed by the Republican-led state legislature that would’ve forced local sheriffs — who run county jails in North Carolina — to cooperate with ICE and hand over inmates suspected of immigration violations.

Cooper said the way the law was written was unconstitutional and would’ve opened up the sheriffs to lawsuits, while also making them take on federal duties rather than focusing on their main jobs. Whatley, however, said that resulted in immigrants being arrested on charges, but then being allowed to bond out, and sometimes fleeing the country.

“Elections have consequences,” Whatley said Friday. “And I think in this election there is no area where you will see bigger consequences than what is going to happen in terms of illegal immigration.”

One of the Whatley supporters who spoke at Friday’s event was Chris Storie, who was injured in 2011 on vacation with family in the Outer Banks when an undocumented immigrant from Honduras crashed into her car. Her brother died in the crash. The man was let out on bail while awaiting trial on drunk driving charges, she said, and fled the country.

WRAL previously interviewed Storie in 2023, about one of the bills Cooper vetoed that would’ve made sheriffs cooperate with ICE.

“I wanted to see him in a courtroom,” Storie said Friday. “I wanted to see him face justice. … I never got the chance to tell him — I don't think he would have cared — but it would make me feel better to let him know what he did to my family.”

As governor in 2024, Cooper supported legislation in the U.S. Senate that would’ve amped up funding for border security, created new pathways to legal status for people already in the country, and speed up the process for asylum claims for people arriving at the border requesting entry while also increasing the standards required of them to receive it.

The bill was framed as a bipartisan immigration reform package that had priorities for Republicans and Democrats alike. But Trump was running for president at the time, and he had been making Biden’s lack of action on immigration a key part of his campaign, so he pressured Republicans in Congress not to pass it.

Whatley was chairman of the Republican National Committee at the time and also pressed GOP officials to oppose the plan, which Cooper’s campaign noted in a statement to WRAL Friday: “Roy Cooper believes our country must have a secure border and was a strong supporter of the toughest border security bill in decades that Michael Whatley opposed and helped torpedo,” a Cooper campaign spokesman said.

Whatley declined to take questions from the media after his event Friday. His campaign spokesman later wrote to WRAL: “Roy Cooper endorsed Joe Biden’s open-border policies and Michael Whatley endorses Trump’s secure borders policies. Michael will make it a priority to promote legislation that keeps our borders secure, even if another radical open-borders President were to be elected so that illegal aliens and dangerous illicit drugs don’t run rampant across our borders.”

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is looking to spend up to $2 million on robot dogs, according to a federal procurement notice.

The Boston Dynamic SPOT Robots will help "support public safety and law enforcement operations by providing a remotely operated robotic capability for inspection, situational awareness, and hazard assessment in environments that may pose risks to personnel," according to the notice.

The technology is also used by the Secret Service. In 2024, the company's robot dogs were seen patrolling Mar-A-Lago in social media videos that went viral.

The robot dogs, which are equipped with 360-degree cameras and can open doors, are also used by police departments across the country.

They cannot attack like a normal police dog, but they do have extendable arms.

In a video posted by the Los Angeles Police Department in 2023, the device is shown examining a crime scene for guns and explosives.

The procurement notice said the robotic dogs will help with securing the border and infrastructure security.

"This capability helps improve officer safety, supports informed operational decision-making, and enhances DHS’s ability to respond to incidents involving dangerous, confined, unstable, or difficult-to-access areas," the notice stated.

text:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit has delivered another major legal blow to the Trump administration's immigration enforcement strategy, ruling that immigrants who entered the United States unlawfully years ago cannot automatically be held without bond under a law the government has increasingly relied upon since 2025.

In a 2-1 decision issued Friday, the Philadelphia-based appeals court upheld orders requiring the release of two longtime U.S. residents who had been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) without bond hearings. The court concluded that their detention violated both the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and constitutional due process protections.

The ruling adds to a growing split among federal appellate courts over whether the administration can use a border detention statute to hold immigrants arrested years after entering the country, a conflict that increasingly appears destined for Supreme Court review.

Read More on Politics

Newsweek reached out to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Department of Justice (DOJ) for comment Friday morning and is awaiting responses.

What the Case Is About

The case involved Gabriel Antonio Buele Morocho, an Ecuadorian national who entered the U.S. in 2001, and Wanderson Lopes De Andrade, a Brazilian national who entered in 2014. Both were arrested by ICE years later and placed into mandatory detention under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Traditionally, immigrants found living in the U.S. after entering without inspection were generally detained under a separate provision, Section 1226(a), which allows immigration judges to consider release on bond if the individual is not considered a danger to the community or a flight risk.

Beginning in 2025, however, the government expanded its use of mandatory detention, arguing that immigrants who had never been formally admitted to the United States could be held without bond while their removal proceedings continued.

The Third Circuit rejected that interpretation.

"Because their detentions without hearings violated the Immigration and Nationality Act ('INA') and due process, we will affirm," Judge Patty Shwartz wrote for the majority.

What Is the Mandatory Detention Policy?

At the heart of the dispute is a section of immigration law that requires detention of certain noncitizens who are "seeking admission" to the U.S. and are found not clearly entitled to enter.

The administration argued that people who entered illegally and never received formal admission remain "applicants for admission" and can therefore be detained under the mandatory detention provision regardless of how long they have lived in the country.

The Third Circuit disagreed, holding that the phrase "seeking admission" refers to people actively trying to gain entry into the country, not individuals who crossed the border years earlier and were later arrested in the U.S. interior.

The court said Congress's use of the word "seeking" implies a present and ongoing effort to gain admission. The judges concluded that immigrants already living in the United States are not in a continuous state of attempting to enter the country.

As a result, the court held that such individuals generally must be processed under Section 1226(a), making them eligible to request bond hearings.

"The policy at the heart of these cases reflects a radical interpretation of the law, and marks a major shift from how the government has applied the law over the past several decades," Jennifer Koh, a law professor at Pepperdine University, told Newsweek.

"If upheld, it would give immigration authorities the power to incarcerate people based solely on the fact that they entered the country unlawfully--no matter how long they have lived in the country or what their ties are. It provides the government with a significant tool in its mass deportation efforts. It also has serious implications for how the courts understand due process for noncitizens."

Due Process Concerns

The Third Circuit also ruled that the government's detention policy violated the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause.

The court stressed that people who have lived in the U.S. for years possess constitutional protections that do not apply in the same way to someone apprehended immediately after crossing the border.

Citing Supreme Court precedent, the panel noted that due process protections extend to all persons physically present in the U.S., regardless of immigration status. The judges found that denying detainees any opportunity to demonstrate they are not dangerous and not likely to flee created an unacceptable risk of wrongful detention.

Other Courts Have Reached Similar Conclusions

The Third Circuit is not alone. The First, Second, Sixth, Seventh, Ninth, Tenth and Eleventh Circuits have also concluded that Section 1225(b)(2)(A) generally does not authorize mandatory detention of immigrants arrested years after entering the United States.

Several of those rulings have already generated petitions asking the Supreme Court to intervene.

"Although many appeals courts have found the policy unlawful, the government has still detained record numbers of noncitizens in the past year under this controversial interpretation of the law," Koh said. "It has done this by transferring immigrants to areas in which court rulings that support the policy exist -- for instance, by moving individuals from California to Texas. Also, in a troubling number of cases, the immigration agency appears to have refused to follow court orders altogether."

The Courts That Sided With the Government

Not every federal appeals court agrees, with the Fifth and Eighth Circuits adopting the administration's position, ruling that Section 1225(b)(2)(A) does authorize mandatory detention for immigrants who entered unlawfully and later were arrested inside the country.

Those decisions concluded that Congress intended the mandatory detention provision to apply broadly to anyone who had never been formally admitted to the United States.

The split means immigration detainees can face different legal standards depending on where they are arrested and prosecuted.

Dissent Warns of Different Treatment for Illegal Entrants

Judge Jennifer Lee 'Jenn' Mascott dissented in the Third Circuit case, arguing that Congress intended to eliminate distinctions between immigrants who presented themselves for inspection and those who crossed the border undetected.

"The majority opinion holds that although aliens approaching the United States at an authorized border entry point may be held without bond, aliens slipping undetected past the border may not," Mascott wrote.

Her dissent echoed arguments the administration has advanced in courts around the country and highlighted the deep divide that could ultimately draw the Supreme Court into the dispute.

Why This Could Head to the Supreme Court

The existence of a direct conflict among federal appeals courts is one of the most common reasons the Supreme Court agrees to hear a case.

The Third Circuit emphasized the disagreement among the circuits throughout its opinion and noted that petitions for Supreme Court review have already been filed in several of the related cases.

The issue is also nationally significant because it affects a major component of the administration's interior immigration enforcement strategy and has implications for potentially large numbers of immigrants who entered the country without inspection but have lived in the U.S. for years.

The government could seek rehearing before the full Third Circuit, but legal observers are likely to focus on whether the Justice Department instead asks the Supreme Court to resolve the question once and for all. A High Court decision would establish a nationwide rule determining whether immigrants arrested long after entering the country may be held without bond under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) or must instead be given access to bond hearings under Section 1226(a).

The company’s founder, Marcella Burke, served in the first Trump administration as a lawyer for the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of the Interior.

text:
CHICAGO — Rep. Mike Quigley, D-Ill., likened the entryway to Chicago’s immigration court to the gates of hell. To reporters, he invoked the ominous quote that appears in Dante’s “Inferno” on signage before souls enter the underworld.

“Abandon all hope, ye who enter here,” Quigley said. “That’s what I saw firsthand today: a sense that there is absolutely no hope under this kind of Trump justice system for the least fortunate, for the most vulnerable.”

An absence of hope was palpable among the immigration attorneys, advocates and lawmakers who attended hearings on Wednesday for the most vulnerable of undocumented immigrants: unaccompanied minors.

But the specific cohort of minors who came before Immigration Court Judge Shawn Abraham on Wednesday, advocates and court observers say, reflects a shift in the administration’s deportation drive. The minors who President Donald Trump once indicated he meant to protect with his hard-line border policies — unaccompanied children who are victims of abuse, neglect or abandonment — have now become the target.

MS NOW watched for two hours as more than a dozen children, some as young as 12, attended their immigration court hearings, competing for space with the hundreds of adults and families lining hallways to attend “mega-master” hearings. Such hearings, which cram dozens of unrepresented undocumented immigrants into a single courtroom at the same time, have become yet another vehicle the administration has adopted to accelerate deportations.

Nearly all of the children who attended Wednesday’s hearing had pending applications for a status adjustment to classify them as “Special Immigrant Juveniles,” a category reserved for young victims of abuse, abandonment or parental neglect who would be at risk if returned to their country of origin. The classification was created in 2008 as a provision of the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act. In past administrations, even a pending application for an SIJ classification was enough not only to delay a deportation order but perhaps to put a child on an expedited path toward citizenship. The Trump administration rescinded that policy in April. As of June, more than 33,000 SIJ petitions were awaiting review, according to quarterly data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

With the rescission, attorneys say, minors who would typically appear in court three or four times a year are returning every two weeks, an accelerated pace that aids the administration’s effort to fast-track deportations.

The effects of the rescission were clear as Abraham, emotionless and mechanical, issued removal orders virtually to a majority of the children in his courtroom, even as their attorneys presented Illinois state court findings that sending the children back to their native countries would not be in their best interest.

Among the children who received a removal order was a 12-year-old wearing a baggy white Air Jordan T-shirt, who fidgeted with a toy handed to him by his immigration advocate. He entered the country when he was 10, and on Wednesday he sat expressionless as Abraham told him through a translator that he would be removed to his home country of El Salvador.

The boy’s advocate, facilitated by the Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights, offered Abraham several pleas as she protested the decision: He is a “vulnerable, tender-age child” who has experienced trauma; an Illinois state judge determined reunification is not a “viable option” for him, as his parents abandoned him; and his safety would be threatened if he were returned to El Salvador.

Abraham, glancing around through his Webex screen as the advocate spoke, was unmoved and told the 12-year-old that he would be returned to his home country, though his attorney could appeal the decision to the Board of Immigration Appeals, or BIA. That board, like the immigration court itself, operates under the executive branch, not the judicial.

Quigley, who sat in court throughout most of the proceedings, objected strongly to Abraham’s decision to appear virtually, a departure from his predecessor Elizabeth Crites, who was fired by the Trump administration last month after five years of service. Abraham is a member of the Illinois State Bar and last year served in the Cook County State Attorney’s Office in Chicago.

“I have a plausible theory for why the administrator this morning wasn’t there in person,” Quigley said. “It would be virtually impossible for anyone, even someone without a soul, to look a kid in the eye and say, ‘I’m sending you back, without your parents, without anyone, with absolutely nothing there, without any justice done.’”

The 12-year-old was one of five migrant children represented by Laura Smith, the executive director of the Children’s Legal Center, who received removal orders despite having pending applications for Special Immigrant Juvenile Status. She described her young clients as “devastated.”

“They came here because they’re terrified. They have faced horrors in their home country, and they’re coming for protection, and they qualify for that protection,” Smith said. “They’re doing everything right, they’re following the law, and yet they’re going to be taken back to a situation that they fled from, a situation that harmed them.”

Smith’s organization, the Children’s Legal Center, is one of roughly 100 legal service providers that have been adversely affected by the Trump administration’s decision to end a federal contract with the Acacia Center for Justice, which had provided counsel to more than 20,000 unaccompanied migrant children.

“It’s an extreme effect on our ability to do our job,” Smith said. “Without the funding, we can’t hire new people, we can’t actually pay the people who we currently have, and so we’re not taking on new cases.”

The Office of Refugee Resettlement, which oversees unaccompanied minors, instead sought to award a $150 million contract to Burke Law Group, a Texas-based firm with 26 employees, only two of whom list immigration as a practice area. The company’s founder, Marcella Burke, served in the first Trump administration as a lawyer for the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of the Interior. Following backlash, however, the group announced this month it had declined to take on the contract.

More articles

Ultimately, the office awarded the contract to anti-trafficking group Our Rescue. The organization’s website does not list legal counsel among the services it provides — a point that has frustrated groups previously contracted to provide the aid.

“If the children don’t have representation, they will more quickly be ordered removed,” Smith said. “They won’t be able to appeal to the BIA and preserve their due process rights, and they won’t be able to eventually get to an actual court, an Article 3 court, to have that court decide whether the policies of this administration are in violation of the law.”

Smith, along with other immigration attorneys, says June marked a turning point in the pace of the Trump administration’s deportations; they saw a significant increase in the issuance of removal orders.

Joy Olson, a Milwaukee-based child advocate and an Acacia board member, has been observing Chicago juvenile court proceedings for the past 15 months. “Since last spring, I’ve only witnessed one or two removals,” she told MS NOW after the hearing ended. On Wednesday, she saw eight. Data backs the claim.

Immigrants in Chicago’s immigration court saw a 120% increase in the number of removals ordered between March and June, according to TRAC reports. That is four times the national average and the largest spike in the country. While publicly available data does not break down those removals by age, it is evident that the deportation of undocumented children is part of what is helping the government maintain that pace. It’s a departure from Trump’s pledge to pursue the “worst of the worst,” said Illinois Sen. Dick Durbin, who also attended Wednesday’s hearing.

“Do you remember how they explained it? We were going after the worst of the worst: the terrorists, the rapists, the murderers, the child predators,” Durbin said. “I wish the people who made those statements could see what we saw this morning.”

The last case on the docket Wednesday was a high-school-age Guatemalan. There was a delay in finding a translator who spoke K’iche’, a Mayan indigenous language. After Abraham issued his removal order, he rattled off a litany of directives through the translator.

“Sir, stay in communications with your attorney. She has the ability to appeal this decision to a higher court. Your appeal would need to be filed by Sept. 25, 2026,” Abraham said. Then he asked the child if he had any questions.

Unlike the majority of children before the judge that day, the minor spoke up through his translator.

“Yes. Why are you sending me back to Guatemala? What did I do?”

CORRECTION (August 28, 2026, 12:21 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article misstated the organization providing legal representation to one of the minors. The group is The Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights, not the National Immigrant Justice Center.

Kayla McCormick contributed reporting.

text:
The Justice Department filed lawsuits seeking to block laws in four states that allow some state residents without U.S. citizenship to qualify for in-state tuition and financial aid at state colleges and universities.

The DOJ filed suits against Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon and Washington, alleging the states "unconstitutionally discriminate against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rates or scholarships, create incentives for illegal immigration, and reward illegal aliens with benefits that U.S. citizens are not eligible for," the department said in a statement Thursday. The department also claimed the laws discriminate against out-of-state students who are citizens.

"As of today, we have now sued 21 states who we allege were thwarting Congress's clear prohibition on placing aliens over citizens. Our efforts will not cease until President Trump's promise is fulfilled: illegal aliens will not receive benefits denied to American citizens," Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr., said in a statement announcing the lawsuits.

"This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens," Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department's Civil Division said in a statement on Thursday. "This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country."

Arizona, Oregon and Washington have vowed to fight the lawsuits in court. New Mexico's governor's office did not immediately respond to ABC News' request for comment.

The Justice Department is seeking to block the laws, regardless of whether the residents are in the U.S. legally and argues that the state laws conflict with federal immigration laws.

States vow to fight the lawsuits

In Arizona, the Justice Department targeted Proposition 308, a 2022 voter-approved law that allows Arizona high school graduates to qualify for in-state tuition at Arizona's public universities and community colleges regardless of their immigration status, according to state law and the attorney general's office.

To qualify, the student must have attended an Arizona high school for at least two years and graduated from an Arizona high school or received an equivalent credential in the state, according to the state's attorney general.

Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes vowed to fight the lawsuit, claiming the government's complaint rests on a "faulty premise."

"The federal government has now sued 21 states for letting Dreamers who attended school in places like Arizona be able to afford a college education at our state's community colleges and universities," Mayes said in a statement. "Fundamentally, this is about state's rights and I will vigorously defend Arizona's right to set its own rules, especially ones that are passed by voters themselves."

In New Mexico, a 2025 law allows some state residents to qualify for in-state tuition and state-funded financial aid regardless of their immigration status, according to the statute.

Non-citizens who qualify include those who have attended a secondary educational institution in New Mexico for at least one year and either graduated from a New Mexico high school or received a high school equivalency credential in New Mexico, according to the law.

The law went into effect in July 2025.

New Mexico's governor's office directed ABC News to its Higher Education Department, which said it had not yet received the official lawsuit as of Thursday but is aware the suit has been announced.

"As we continue to review the information, we remain focused on our long‑standing commitment to expanding higher education pathways for New Mexicans. Our colleges and universities play a vital role in strengthening the state's workforce, building talent pipelines, and ensuring that students have access to opportunities that support both individual and statewide success," the department said.

"We are committed to ensuring that New Mexicans have reliable, structured pathways to afford and access higher education. We will continue to uphold our mission of supporting students, strengthening our workforce, and advancing educational opportunity across the state," the department said.

In Oregon, a 2013 law called the Tuition Equity Act allows some students who are residents of the state but not U.S. citizens to pay resident tuition and fees at public universities, according to state law.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said young people who grew up in Oregon, go to Oregon schools, and graduate from Oregon high schools "are part of our communities and part of our future," in a statement to ABC News about the suit.

"I will continue to stand up for their opportunity to pursue an education and build a life here. Rather than focus on affordability and reduce costs for Oregon families, the federal administration seems determined to attack state laws that have been successful for a decade," Kotek said.

In Washington, non-citizens can qualify for in-state tuition after living in the state for at least one year before entering an institution of higher education and if they provide an affidavit indicating they will file an application to become a permanent resident and a willingness to engage in other activities necessary to acquire citizenship, according to state law.

"Washington state won't be bullied into changing how we provide opportunities for young people in our state. We'll see them in court, and we expect to win," Gov. Bob Ferguson said in a statement to ABC News.

text:
ICE expanding detention center in Batavia

ICE is calling for a "temporary detention structure," which in other places has meant tents. Meanwhile, County Executive Mark Poloncarz has nixed a Homeland Security job fair at the downtown convention center.

Share on

The ICE detention facility in Batavia. Photo by J. Dale Shoemaker.

The Trump administration is moving to award a no-bid contract to expand the ICE detention center in Batavia to accommodate a surge in arrests of migrants.

At the insistence of Erie County Executive Mark Poloncarz, however, the agency has been thwarted in an effort to use the Buffalo Convention Center to host a job fair next week.

According to a notice on the federal government’s contracting website, ICE plans to hire the Virginia-based firm Akima Infrastructure Protection to construct “a temporary detention structure” to house 100 detainees on the campus of the Batavia facility. ICE’s current detention center has a capacity of 650 but averaged 730 detainees in recent months.

The overcrowding follows a surge in arrests. ICE data through Aug. 5 shows arrests across upstate New York spiked from 788 during President Biden’s last 12 months in office to 6,216 during Trump’s 19 months since returning to Washington. Seventy-two percent arrested during Trump’s time had no criminal record.

The federal notice does not describe what a temporary detention structure entails, but Akima has been hired for similar projects, including a “tent city” for migrants in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.

ICE tents have appeared elsewhere, too. A year ago, The Wall Street Journal reported that ICE had “given priority to erecting thousands of tents, or ‘hardened soft-sided facilities,’ as quickly as possible to expand detention capacity quickly at U.S. military bases and adjoining bricks-and-mortar ICE jails.”

In Batavia, the federal government plans to hire Akima as a sole-source contractor and is not conducting a bidding process for the new facility. Akima Infrastructure was also recently awarded the multi-million dollar federal contract to manage the detention facility in a transition from its sister company, Akima Global Services. That agreement runs for a decade. Both firms are subsidiaries of NANA, an Alaskan firm owned by indigenous Alaskans.

ICE justified the lack of bidding by stating in the notice that only Akima could build a temporary facility for migrants “without unacceptable risk to [agency] operations.” ICE is giving companies until 5 p.m. today to file a protest to the no-bid award to Akima.

Few other details are available. An ICE spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. The outlet Project Salt Box first reported on the contract notice Thursday.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a July statement it planned to construct a “new hard-sided detention facility on federal property” in response to New York restricting local law enforcement from cooperating with the agency. The Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, which took effect Tuesday, nullifies cooperation agreements ICE signed with local police and sheriffs. In Western New York, the Niagara County Sheriff and the Village of Allegany provided detention space for women at local jails. The Batavia facility is currently men only.

Another notice posted on the federal contracting website indicates that ICE may purchase additional land for a future expansion of the Batavia facility. That report said ICE planned to hire the California-based firm First American Title Insurance Company for “real estate title abstract, escrow and settlement services” in Florida, Arizona and Batavia at a cost of $240,000.

“These properties are required to meet operational requirements for modernizing and enhancing immigration detention and enforcement capabilities for ICE,” the notice read. “The existing processing centers in these locations will be expanded to enable additional administrative, medical, training and detention facilities and space.”

The Batavia facility is surrounded by farms, an industrial park and Interstate 90.

Genesee County officials said they’re being kept in the dark.

“I am learning of the expansion from what the media has been reporting,” county manager Matt Landers told Investigative Post.

Felipe Oltramari, the county planning director, said ICE would not need any planning approvals from the county or Town of Batavia. The facility may require a state environmental review, Oltramari said, but added ICE could circumvent that process.

“There is a possibility that [Homeland Security] undertakes the project as an emergency action which could, in part or entirely, bypass the environmental review,” he said.

ICE has also shut down the immigration court that was attached to its Batavia detention center, according to immigration attorneys who spoke with Investigative Post. Immigration judges that practiced there have been moved to Buffalo. Several rooms are now being used for detainees to attend their court hearings virtually via WebEx. It’s not clear what ICE plans to do with the rest of the space.

Aaron Krupp, an advocate for detained migrants with Justice for Migrant Families, said the expansion could lead to more ICE arrests around the state and region.

“As history tells us, ‘If they build it, they will fill it,’” Krupp said. “An ICE prison expansion means more ICE activity terrorizing our communities. It means more kidnappings, more families torn apart, more children without parents.”

Gov. Kathy Hochul is concerned, too.

In a July letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Hochul questioned which detention facilities might be expanded in the state and why.

“New Yorkers, like all Americans, deserve honest answers about what their federal government is doing in their communities. And I demand your department provide that transparency,” Hochul wrote.

Mullin has not responded to the letter. In a statement Thursday, a Hochul spokesperson said the governor believes the expansion of Batavia is unwarranted.

“There is no need for DHS to move forward with expanding any detention facilities in the state,” the spokesperson said. “New Yorkers deserve transparency from their federal government, and the Governor will continue to demand answers.”

Meanwhile, the Department of Homeland Security — of which ICE and Border Patrol are part — had planned a career fair at the Buffalo Convention Center for Sept. 1 and 2. The agency said it planned to recruit for immigration services, intelligence, law enforcement and mission support roles, along with jobs related to business operations, finance, cybersecurity and human resources.

Late Thursday, however, Visit Buffalo Niagara President and CEO Patrick Kaler said he cancelled the event, at Poloncarz’s request.

“The Buffalo Convention Center is a publicly owned community asset and I do not believe it should be used to support recruitment efforts that are inconsistent with the values we have repeatedly expressed as a welcoming community,” Poloncarz said.

He added: “I strongly encouraged [the Buffalo Niagara Convention Center Management Corporation] leadership to cancel the contract and inform DHS that the Buffalo Convention Center will not serve as the host site for this event. This is exactly what has occurred.”

Prior to the cancellation, the event raised concerns from local activists who oppose ICE operating in Buffalo. The group Evict ICE from 250 Delaware — which wants landlord Uniland to not renew ICE’s lease for office space at 250 Delaware Avenue — released a statement Thursday decrying the recruitment event.

“Hosting an ICE recruitment event at a taxpayer-funded convention center is antithetical to the stated plans of elected officials and community leaders to revitalize downtown Buffalo,” Harper Bishop, campaign coordinator for the Evict ICE group, said in a statement.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to clarify the relationship between Akima Infrastructure Protection and Akima Global Services.

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Justice on Thursday sued Oregon, Arizona, New Mexico and Washington over laws that allow immigrants in the country without legal status to pay in-state college tuition in the states where they live.

President Donald Trump’s administration has now sued 21 states over such laws, which enable noncitizen students who meet certain requirements access to in-state tuition at public colleges and universities, regardless of their immigration status.

The lawsuits argue that these policies allow students without legal status to pay drastically lower tuition for public education than U.S. citizens from other states. They also come as the administration aims to curb benefits that could be extended to immigrants more broadly.

“Over 30 years ago, Congress made clear that States cannot put illegal aliens before our Nation’s own citizens,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. said in a statement announcing the four additional lawsuits. “By granting illegal aliens in-state tuition, Washington, Oregon, New Mexico, and Arizona are pushing citizens to the side and ignoring federal law. No more.”

Advocates for the policy of allowing in-state tuition regardless of immigration status say it does not bestow any advantages not available to the students’ peers in their home states.

Meanwhile, in five of the DOJ’s lawsuits — against Texas, Kentucky, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Illinois — courts have already struck down the state laws. Illinois was the only one of those states that did not join with the federal government but instead defended its laws.

Lawsuits are also pending in California, Colorado, Connecticut, Kansas, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont and Virginia.

WASHINGTON (CN) — Milo Yiannopoulos, the controversial right-wing commentator who has called for “total immunity” for federal agents conducting mass deportations, has been detained by immigration enforcement and will be removed from the country.

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed Friday afternoon that Yiannopoulos, who is from the United Kingdom, was in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement pending deportation. The agency shared a mugshot of the conservative provocateur to social media, writing that Yiannopoulos “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws.”

A supporter of President Donald Trump during his 2016 campaign, Yiannopoulos had under the second Trump administration been a vocal proponent of the president’s mass deportation effort, urging the White House to go to extremes to remove people here illegally from the country.

“Total legal immunity for ICE agents when they’re on duty,” Yiannopoulos wrote in September 2025, months before immigration agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens in the streets of Minneapolis. The former Breitbart editor and campaign adviser to rapper and onetime presidential candidate Kanye West also said last summer that supporters of the Trump administration must “insist” that it “deport millions and millions of people.”

“Without that, nothing else matters,” wrote Yiannopoulos.

ICE agents arrested Yiannopoulos on Thursday at Louisiana’s Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport and according to Homeland Security a final order of removal was issued by an immigration judge in July.

Yiannopoulos, 41, first entered the U.S. on a legal visa in 2019. He will remain in federal custody until he’s deported, DHS said.

“Being in detention is a choice,” the agency wrote in a statement — using language it has long employed to discuss mass deportations. “The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”

Yiannopoulos, though a major figure in the right-wing media sphere during Trump’s first administration, has since found himself at odds with other conservative figures such as Laura Loomer, an ally of the president who’s chafed at Yiannopoulos’ recent stint as an intern for former Georgia Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene.

Writing in a post on X Friday, Loomer said that Yiannopoulos’ arrest was “a great day for America.” She took credit for reporting his immigration status to the Trump administration.

“I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the U.S. illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” said Loomer, invoking an often-used nickname for the former Republican lawmaker who has fallen out with Trump.

Yiannopoulos first rose to prominence in 2014, where as an editor at Breitbart he was a central figure to the Gamergate controversy — an online harassment campaign against women which stemmed from video game culture and formed part of the groundwork for the alt-right political movement.

BuzzFeed News reported in 2017 that Yiannopoulos had worked with white nationalists to workshop story ideas while at Breitbart. He’d left the publication that year after video emerged of him saying sex between 13-year-old boys and adults could be “perfectly consensual.” Yiannopoulos said at the time that he condemned sexual abuse.

Yiannopoulos most recently worked on Kanye West’s ill-fated 2024 presidential campaign. He’s claimed that while working for West he arranged a 2022 dinner between Trump and far-right commentator Nick Fuentes in an effort to make the then-Republican presidential candidate look bad.

title: Op-Ed: ICE enforcement in our communities - InDepthNH.org
description:
In my view, under the current administration immigration enforcement has become far too aggressive and too often insufficiently restrained by due process.
These are not concerns that should be dismissed simply because the federal government has legitimate authority to enforce our immigration laws.
At the same time, I do not believe the answer is to abolish immigration enforcement.
The answer to abuses by ICE is not to abolish immigration enforcement, but to fundamentally reform how we carry it out.
But right now, I would support dismantling ICE entirely and creating a new immigration enforcement agency since that seems what is necessary to achieve those reforms.
text:
By Rep. PAUL BERCH, D-Westmoreland

ICE activities in Troy and Keene have increased the already high level of concern about ICE activity in our communities. A constituent recently asked for my thoughts, particularly in light of these events.

ICE did not create the American deportation system. Most of ICE’s fundamental legal authority comes from laws enacted before ICE existed—particularly the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 and major amendments enacted in 1986 and 1996. What has changed dramatically from administration to administration is who is targeted for enforcement, how aggressively those laws are enforced, what priorities are established, and how much state and local governments cooperate.

In my view, under the current administration immigration enforcement has become far too aggressive and too often insufficiently restrained by due process. The concerns are serious: arrests of people with no criminal record, including asylum seekers and people legally authorized to work; allegations of racial profiling; arrests arising from routine traffic encounters; inadequate access to lawyers and meaningful bond hearings; troubling conditions and medical care in detention; and efforts to remove people before they have a meaningful opportunity to pursue their legal claims. These are not concerns that should be dismissed simply because the federal government has legitimate authority to enforce our immigration laws.

At the same time, I do not believe the answer is to abolish immigration enforcement. The United States has both the right and the responsibility to enforce its immigration laws, protect its borders, and remove individuals who pose genuine threats to public safety or national security. But enforcing the law and respecting constitutional rights are not competing principles. We can—and must—do both.

The answer to abuses by ICE is not to abolish immigration enforcement, but to fundamentally reform how we carry it out. It may be possible to reform ICE, with stronger oversight and accountability, meaningful due process, humane treatment of those in federal custody, and clear enforcement priorities focused on serious criminals and genuine threats to public safety and national security.

But right now, I would support dismantling ICE entirely and creating a new immigration enforcement agency since that seems what is necessary to achieve those reforms. The name of the agency and its organizational structure are far less important than its mission, its culture, and the safeguards governing its conduct. We need an agency that enforces our immigration laws firmly and effectively, while respecting constitutional rights, due process, and human dignity.

A nation committed to the rule of law must insist that the government obey the law while it enforces it. In a Constitutional republic founded on principles of human dignity, the laws in question and the enforcement of those laws must be both just and equitable.

I will work to hasten the time when the United States embraces immigration reform that secures our borders, smoothly processes refugees and asylum seekers, meets the needs of employers, provides a path to citizenship, and respects the humanity of all people.

Rep. Paul Berch

Cheshire – 06 (Westmoreland, Chesterfield, Hinsdale)

Ranking Democrat – NH House Judiciary Committee

title: California senators demand investigation of ICE trying to enter Sacramento law firm
description:
Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla are demanding a federal investigation into U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s recent attempt to inspect a Sacramento immigration law firm without a warrant.
Employees later said an ICE agent who entered the front lobby of the law firm claimed officers had a list from Washington D.C., that said people lived at the address.
The ICE agent then reportedly warned that officers could return at 3 a.m. and break windows to enter if they received follow-up orders.
The statements differ in details, but all say that ICE officers arrived at a “target address” for people they planned to arrest, were unaware it was a law firm and departed after learning that information.
Video footage shows the officers in the parking lot of the law firm for at least 43 minutes.
text:
California U.S. Sens. Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla are demanding a federal investigation into U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s recent attempt to inspect a Sacramento immigration law firm without a warrant.

In a letter sent Thursday afternoon to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and ICE, the two senators request that the agencies investigate the federal agents’ actions and provide specifics on the purpose of the operation. The letter, first shared with The Sacramento Bee, called DHS’ description of the incident thus far “troubling and unsatisfactory.”

“ICE’s conduct here is another example of a broader, systemic effort by this administration to intimidate immigrant communities and the attorneys and legal representatives who represent them,” the senators said in their letter. “We refuse to tolerate these efforts to target law firms and organizations based solely on who their clients may be or their practice areas.”

The incident unfolded around the morning of Aug. 14 when multiple ICE officers arrived at the Morris Law Group office in North Natomas. Employees later said an ICE agent who entered the front lobby of the law firm claimed officers had a list from Washington D.C., that said people lived at the address.

He asked to tour the office for beds, but was repeatedly denied access after failing to provide a warrant. The ICE agent then reportedly warned that officers could return at 3 a.m. and break windows to enter if they received follow-up orders. Judicial warrants are needed to enter non-public areas of a business.

DHS has provided three written statements to The Bee since the incident. The statements differ in details, but all say that ICE officers arrived at a “target address” for people they planned to arrest, were unaware it was a law firm and departed after learning that information.

Padilla and Schiff, in their letter, said they are “baffled” by that premise. They note that a Google search of the address shows it is a legal practice and the law firm’s name appears in large, bold letters on the front of the building.

Video footage shows the officers in the parking lot of the law firm for at least 43 minutes. They are parked directly in front of the building for the majority of that time.

“It is clear that some DHS enforcement personnel wrongly believe they can enter individuals’ private properties, including places of business, without valid, judicial warrants required by the Fourth Amendment,” the senators said in their letter.

Among other requests, the senators demanded responses to the purpose of the Aug. 14 operation, why officers failed to secure a warrant and ask to tour for beds, which ICE field office led the operation and if they will commit to investigating the allegation that agents could potentially return at 3 a.m. The senators also insisted on answers about the alleged list from Washington, D.C., including who provided the list, what factors were considered in creating it and a list of offices and officials involved in the process.

They requested responses by Sept. 11, citing the serious allegations of the operation.

Schiff and Padilla are one of several elected leaders who have publicly criticized ICE’s actions. Last week, California Assemblymember Maggy Krell, D-Sacramento, submitted a Freedom of Information Act request seeking communications and records of the agents and agencies involved in the operation.
